articles.title: Psychologists want us to rethink what we ask about school violence
articles.summary: Rather than neatly condense all the violence and trace it to one root cause, psychologists choose to ask the difficult questions about each individual case. Each child in conflict with the law is not…

blocks.text: This is Part 1 of a two-part story.

The kids aren’t alright. Only a few months into the school year, multiple cases of school violence have been reported throughout the Philippines, where the students themselves are the perpetrators inflicting harm on their school community. The most recent incident in Zamboanga was a school shooting that resulted in the death of two students: one who was fatally shot by his schoolmate, while the other was the shooter himself, who, after live streaming his violent acts on social media, ended his own life.

These incidents have alarmed psychologists and mental health practitioners, especially those who work with minors and young Filipinos. But rather than neatly condense all the violence and attribute it to one root cause, they choose to ask the difficult questions about each individual case. They want to understand each student not just as a perpetrator, but as a highly vulnerable person.

“When I heard about the school violence, I immediately asked, ‘What was happening to the teenager’s life that made her or him to be in that position?’” said psychologist Jannah Trixie Cuevas. “What was happening at home? What was happening in the school? Why did it happen in school? What comes to their mind before they started getting the gun? Did someone influence them? Did someone try to manipulate them?”

“No student will do that if they can handle things properly,” psychologist Arnel Sarte Jr. said. “We have to ask: What are they experiencing that pushed them to do that? What are they carrying on their own, until they reach a breaking point?”

Both Cuevas and Sarte work with Sapphire Clinics East Inc., a Filipino-owned rehabilitation and psychological services network in Metro Manila. In the two years they have been operating, the clinic has already handled more than 2,700 clients with a median age of 14 years old. In their work, they respond to warning signs in children and minors who exhibit mental health issues in order to prevent any “breaking points” from happening.

As minors, children and teenagers’ brains are not yet fully developed. Their prefrontal cortex, the part of their brain which manages decision making, emotion processing and control, and impulse regulation, will only fully mature around their mid-20s. Until then, they are “like sponges,” absorbing everything around them.

“Anything that they’re experiencing at school, at home, also what they’re seeing online, they will absorb quickly. Imagine all the risks that they can absorb while they’re growing up,” Sarte said. “If they’re exposed to bullying, invalidation, pressure, that can make them do things they don’t want to. As kids, their brain isn’t fully developed. They don’t have enough ways to properly process things.”

Processing difficult experiences and complex emotions with children is crucial for parents and schools. It is what will save their children from internalizing and carrying their struggles on their own to the point where they cannot bear it anymore. Once a child reaches a breaking point, they can either implode or explode; they can hurt themselves or hurt others.

In schools, experts say teachers and administrators are becoming more observant and attuned to the mental health warning signs and calls for help their students are exhibiting. Hannah Pellejo Jara, CEO and founder of Sapphire Clinics East, says that educational institutions have been partnering with them for more mental health support for their students because there are times when the school is no longer equipped to handle them.

“What they’re saying is there’s really a shift with the mental health of children,” she shared. “In their guidance office, they have concerns. That’s why they’re partnering with us. What we have seen are suicidal cases, depression cases. A lot of it is family conflict, I would say. We’re seeing a lot of anxiety, panic, and anger management, even in kids.”

Questions that seem reasonable to ask about this situation are, “Why are they like that?” or “What’s wrong with them?” But psychologists propose more productive questions that avoid connotations of defectiveness or blaming the child for things they perhaps could not control. “What are they going through?” “What is their family history like?” or “What did they experience?” are questions that instead seek to understand the child and see them as a whole person.
Guided by the biopsychosocial model, psychologists check the different dimensions of the child to understand their mental health vulnerabilities.

First is the biological factor, specifically their genes, brain chemistry, hormones, and overall physical health. Is their family vulnerable to mental health disorders? Is there a predisposition toward violence or issues like impulse control?

blocks.caption: [OPINION] If our answer starts at the school gate, we are too late

blocks.text: Second is the psychological factor. If they’re vulnerable to certain disorders, are they prone to being sensitive and emotionally or mentally overwhelmed? Are they moody? How do they cope with struggles and conflict? Do they have triggers?

Third, the social factor. What is their environment like at home? At school? Who are their support systems? Who are their friends? Do they feel supported and validated? What is their family’s socioeconomic situation?
The answers to these questions are the puzzle pieces that form the bigger picture of what burdens a person and has built up inside them.

“For a certain person to develop a disorder, there should be an interaction with the genes, the predispositions, and the social factors or environmental factors that would really nurture the disorder,” Cuevas said. “For example, you cannot inherit gambling itself, but the problems when it comes to impulse control. And then, you get connected with people who usually have problems when it comes to impulse control. It creates more tendencies to develop, but it’s not a guarantee.”

Children with mental health vulnerabilities might not even develop disorders if they have access to adequate support systems and safe spaces at home and in their immediate community. “Sometimes what happens is that they just get worse when the environment, when the kid is repeatedly exposed to triggers,” said Sarte.
What could these triggering environments look like?

“There could be a lot of invalidations at home, a lot of unprocessed [experiences] at home, a lot of negative emotions inside the home that teenagers no longer feel safe at home, I think some part of it is when there’s a lot of violence inside the home,” Cuevas said as examples, looking back on past anxiety, depression, and trauma cases.

These environments normalize aggression and violence and elicit stress over feeling unsafe. “Even though we think that the kids don’t have any reaction to it, something is going on with their minds,” Cuevas warned. “Especially teenagers, this is the age that they are making sense of what’s happening in the world. As they’re making sense of the world, it was normalized to just shout at people, to just be aggressive to people, to just not talk when things are not going well at home. It usually starts with that.”

One effect this has on children can result in mirrored behavior, where a kid mirrors the violence at home by bullying others. Another is the child developing a persistent sense of helplessness, of feeling small and defenseless against those harming them.
Cuevas is worried, however, by how children who experience helplessness could perceive the school violence cases, especially the live streamed Zamboanga shooting.

“For some kids who feel very helpless, very small of themselves, seeing this all over the social media for two to three days, maybe one week, gives them an idea. ‘Oh, I can do it too. For them, for me to feel more powerful,’ that gives them a sense of power again.”

She echoed the calls of fellow psychologists at the Psychological Association of the Philippines for social media users and members of the media to be responsible about their coverage of the incidents, especially with the risk of copycat behavior.

“The child who feels helpless, upon seeing the social media post doing such a thing like that could unconsciously provide a hero [image]. Like holding a gun, everyone bowing their head, they could have a different way of seeing it, ‘I’m more powerful than you guys. Before you were bullying me, before you were saying that I’m small, but now, holding this weapon gives me more power than all of you guys.’”

blocks.caption: [Be The Good] Not another school shooting please

blocks.text: This is what makes the Ateneo de Zamboanga school shooting particularly troubling. According to authorities, the shooter was a “very bright student” whom no one would have expected would do such a thing.
“It’s a wake-up call,” Cuevas said, “that even though someone is still performing, that doesn’t guarantee that your child is doing well emotionally.”

Sarte said this is why we need to be attentive and not so dismissive of early warning signs of mental health issues. Children aren’t just asking for attention or being dramatic — and being depressed or anxious isn’t something they want to happen to or that they set out to do.

And maybe that is what Filipino children need the most: families, schools, and communities that refrain from quick assumptions or dismissive attitudes, and instead are attentive, curious, and concerned about the heavy burdens their young hearts carry. – Rappler.com
Part 2 to be published on Saturday, August 29.
Elise Suarez is a Rappler intern from Puerto Princesa City and a Humanities student of the University of Asia & the Pacific.

articles.title: ARTHACUP draws huge field at Sevina Park
articles.summary: Arthaland, the country’s foremost green developer, took its partnership with the Azkals Development Academy (ADA) to another level by staging ARTHACUP 2026 recently at the DLSU Laguna Football Field…

blocks.text: Arthaland, the country’s foremost green developer, took its partnership with the Azkals Development Academy (ADA) to another level by staging ARTHACUP 2026 recently at the DLSU Laguna Football Field beside Sevina Park in Biñan, Laguna.

The tournament brought together more than 1,100 young players, coaches, parents and guests as Arthaland bolstered its belief that building sustainable communities also means creating opportunities for the next generation.
It is also another way of putting this into practice, supporting young athletes as they develop their skills, confidence, and character through football.
The tournament drew players from ADA clubs and teams from Metro Manila, Southern Luzon and as far as Bacolod and Davao.
The tournament winners were Lingap Leads in the U-5 and U-13 categories, G8 Academy in U-7, LAOS FC in U-9 and Kaya FC in U-11.
“Sustainability goes beyond the environment. It is also about investing in people and
giving the next generation opportunities to grow,” said Pam Go, marketing and
corporate communications unit head of Arthaland.

“Football gives young players the chance to learn how to work as a team, handle challenges, and stay disciplined while enjoying the game. We appreciate Arthaland’s continued support of our young athletes,” said Stephen Schrock of the Azkals Development Academy.
Go added that ARTHACUP 2026 was a natural fit for Sevina Park, where an active and family-oriented lifestyle is part of everyday life.

For many participants, it was their first visit to Sevina Park, an 8.1-hectare community . planned by Sasaki Associates, which dedicated 60 percent of its land to green and open spaces. Its walkable, bicycle-friendly layout gives residents space to exercise, spend time outdoors, garden and gather with family and friends.

articles.title: P1-billion fund revitalizes Project Noah. But they need more help reaching LGUs.
articles.summary: 'We can mainstream the science, the knowledge into the plans of the community,' says disaster risk management expert Mahar Lagmay

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – Project Noah has been revitalized with a P1-billion fund release from the 2026 national budget, half of which will go to up-to-date equipment such as LiDAR drones and the rest to operations and its researchers.
Despite this newfound support to this long-running program, there remains the problem of reaching more local governments with knowledge and maps that scientists generate.

Project Noah is a hazard monitoring program launched in 2012, considered a landmark project in the Philippines’ disaster risk reduction and management. The Rodrigo Duterte administration pulled the plug on the program in 2017, which was then under the Department of Science and Technology. Project Noah did not completely disappear but with its termination, the program lost most of its experts and reach.
Currently, the University of the Philippines Resilience Institute (UPRI) manages Project Noah.

With the new funds, UPRI intends to prioritize using cutting-edge technology. This would allow it to generate higher resolution maps of major river basins, a huge improvement from the maps generated when Project Noah was launched 14 years ago. It will also continue promoting nature-based solutions to disaster risk reduction and management.

Mahar Lagmay, the institute’s executive director, listed down their priority areas in budget allocation such as: simulation of major detention basins, LiDAR drone surveys with educational institutions, native tree-mapping and inventory. Higher resolution is not just a quality issue; with it, UPRI researchers will be able to see where exactly flooding happens in a particular street.
Lagmay said they need help in disseminating information, including reaching more local governments so they can apply science to disaster risk management.

“We can mainstream the science, the knowledge into the plans of the community,” Lagmay said in a mix of Filipino and English on Thursday, August 27. “We want the plans of the community to be in accordance with the vision of the stakeholders.”
Lagmay said Project Noah will continue to prioritize support for the government’s flagship flood mitigation program Oplan Kontra Baha.

“The business of hazards mapping is not just to identify the hazards but more importantly to identify the safest places in the community for development and for citing evacuation centers,” Lagmay said.
According to Lagmay, UPRI has worked with at least 20 local governments on hazard and risk mapping in a span of eight years.
A notable partnership of UPRI was with the Quezon City local government. The result was a city-wide drainage master plan that relied on “science and nature-based solutions to mitigate flooding.”

All local governments UPRI has worked with “were really aggressive” and “wanted to change the system,” said Lagmay. Working with a local government to find ways to mitigate flooding and other hazards takes one to two years.
University of the Philippines President Angelo Jimenez said the university is “not an implementing arm” but only provides the knowledge and resource.
“It’s our mandate to offer this resource to the people,” Jimenez said in the same press briefing. “I believe that because of recent events, there is more appreciation of our work.”
He referred to the P1-billion funding as some sort of recognition, but it will need to be replenished if the government wants to continue Project NOAH. – Rappler.com
Quotes translated to English for brevity.

articles.title: Smart Haven Innovation brings portable smart TV experience to home gaming with SH Vision Series
articles.summary: For gamers who want a dedicated screen without committing an entire room to a permanent gaming setup, Smart Haven Innovation is positioning its SH Vision Lite and SH Vision Pro mobile smart TVs as…

blocks.text: For gamers who want a dedicated screen without committing an entire room to a permanent gaming setup, Smart Haven Innovation is positioning its SH Vision Lite and SH Vision Pro mobile smart TVs as flexible entertainment displays that can accommodate both console gaming and everyday use.

Designed with portability in mind, the two Android-based mobile smart TVs allow users to connect compatible gaming consoles through HDMI while retaining access to Android entertainment features when the gaming session ends.

The SH Vision Lite features a 22-inch in-cell touch display, while the larger SH Vision Pro comes with a 32-inch in-cell touch display. Both models offer a 1920 × 1080 resolution and support HDMI input at up to 1080p/60 Hz for compatible consoles.

Both displays also come with full-function USB Type-C connectivity and an RJ45 Ethernet port, giving users additional options for connecting compatible devices and establishing a wired network connection.
The Vision Lite and Vision Pro each have 8 GB of RAM and 128 GB of internal storage. Both models run Android 13, allowing the displays to function beyond their role as gaming screens.
From gaming to everyday entertainment
The SH Vision series is designed to make the screen part of a broader entertainment setup.

During a gaming session, users can connect a compatible console and use the display as their gaming screen. Once the console is switched off, the touchscreen interface can be used to navigate Android-based content, allowing the same device to transition to other forms of entertainment.
This dual-purpose approach gives users an alternative to conventional fixed gaming monitors or televisions, particularly for households where a permanent gaming setup may not be practical.
Designed to move with the player
Portability is another key feature of the SH Vision series. Both models are equipped with a 14.4 V / 15,000 mAh battery, allowing them to operate away from a fixed power outlet.

For gamers sharing living spaces, the mobile design makes it possible to move the display to an available room or location for a gaming session and relocate it afterward. This can help keep shared spaces flexible while still providing access to a larger, dedicated screen when needed.
The approach also allows users to adapt their gaming environment depending on the occasion, rather than keeping a gaming display permanently positioned in one part of the home.
Connectivity at the center of the experience
With HDMI console support, Android functionality, USB Type-C and Ethernet connectivity, Smart Haven Innovation is positioning the SH Vision Lite and SH Vision Pro as more than portable displays.
The company sees the models as part of a connected home entertainment environment where a single screen can support gaming, streaming, and other Android-based activities while being moved as needed.
The SH Vision Lite and SH Vision Pro are aimed at players who want the flexibility of a gaming display without sacrificing the broader entertainment functions of a smart TV.
For more information and updates on Smart Haven Innovation’s latest models and September announcements, visit Smart Haven Innovation or follow the company on Facebook and Instagram.

articles.title: Lacson proposes defunding persistently non-performing GOCCs
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson raised the possibility of reducing financial support to persistently non-performing government-owned and controlled corporations (GOCCs) instead so the government can…

blocks.text: Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson raised the possibility of reducing financial support to persistently non-performing government-owned and controlled corporations (GOCCs) instead so the government can maximize its limited resources.

Lacson made the proposal during the Development Budget Coordinating Committee (DBCC) briefing on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027 at the Senate on Thursday, August 27, where he asked state economic managers about their policy on GOCCs that still receive yearly subsidies despite continually providing zero revenues or little or no apparent benefit.
Instead of merely reducing their subsidies, Lacson said defunding stubbornly non-performing GOCCs may help the government utilize public funds to other agencies that can generate more revenues.

“What is the new policy of the government on non-performing GOCCs? These are the ones that the national government subsidizes every year but don't give any important revenue or service in return - all expenses and subsidies but no revenues,” Lacson asked during the DBCC briefing.
“Why not just abolish them, or not fund them for that matter? Even if they are not abolished by law, they can no longer function without funding,” he pointed out.

According to Department of Finance (DOF) Secretary Frederick Go, the Governance Commission for GOCCs is considering 21 GOCCs for closure, winding down or absorption by other GOCCs, but the process is "very slow, long and tedious."
Department of Budget and Management (DBM) Secretary Kim Robert de Leon, on the other hand, said they are considering separation incentives for potentially affected personnel.

Lacson said that while he understands the complexities of pushing through with such actions as it may displace staff and personnel manning those GOCCs, he urged state economic managers to come up with contingency plans once they are abolished, considering these are government employees.
The senator said the national government should look into how much it has been subsidizing non-performing GOCCs annually vis-à-vis the country’s tight fiscal space.

“I understand the complexities because there will be staff who will be displaced. What are your contingency plans in case the GOCCs are abolished? These are government employees. Maybe that's one reason why you find difficulty in abolishing these GOCCs. But we cannot afford to consider humanitarian reasons in view of the very tight fiscal space we're having now,” he pointed out.
Questionable lump sums

Also during the DBCC briefing, Lacson questioned why, according to the DBM, the preparation of the 2027 national budget is already considered “execution-ready” when it allows appropriations for “blank” items.
The senator noted there are lump sum allocations of P180-million each for all 17 regions, for evacuations centers.
“But there were no specifics. Much as we would like to believe you, the NEP says otherwise,” Lacson said in response to de Leon’s statement.
Moreover, he noted that these “blank items” were not just present in the 2027 budget.

“And mind you, this is not just for the 2027 NEP. We also saw P100-million lump sums each for all 17 regions. We will ask the DPWH (Department of Public Works and Highways) about this too but since this is part of policy, why did the DBCC allow the budget to fund items that are 'blank,' meaning there are amounts but no specific details?” he pointed out.

De Leon then explained that the agencies would still be required to submit the final details to the DBM before the allocations could be implemented. He also said the Office of Civil Defense (OCD) still has to finalize the list.
But Lacson pointed out that such details should have been submitted during the budget preparation stage.

He also noted that while the OCD estimates the cost of each evacuation center at P75-million, the Philippine Disaster Resilience Foundation (PDRF), one of the private sector groups that worked on Yolanda rehabilitation, along with BPI, constructed an evacuation center in Ibaan, Batangas amounting to P12.7-million.

The PDRF was among the private sector organizations that Lacson worked with during his stint as Presidential Assistant for Rehabilitation and Recovery, where he coordinated efforts to help those affected by Super Typhoon Yolanda (Haiyan).

“How many evacuation centers following the 2013-2014 model can be built with P3.06 billion? The OCD estimates each evacuation center costs P75M, this is quite far from P12.77M. Even accounting for inflation, P75M per evacuation center is quite high,” Lacson said.

articles.title: Review: Nissan Almera VL
articles.summary: Look at our roads, you’ll notice a multitude of crossovers, hybrids and electrified SUVs. All meant to get you from A to B, with a spacious cabin, while economical. The humble sedan seems to have…

blocks.text: Look at our roads, you’ll notice a multitude of crossovers, hybrids and electrified SUVs. All meant to get you from A to B, with a spacious cabin, while economical. The humble sedan seems to have been overlooked, while most have the capability to perform the same task.
The Nissan Almera is a small sedan with a small engine, and at a time where fuel costs remain a major consideration for Filipino motorists, that may actually be one of its biggest advantages.
Upmarket styling

The Almera doesn't look like an economy car. Nissan's V-Motion grille, gloss-black detailing, LED headlights, LED signature daytime running lamps and LED tail lamps give the sedan a sharp, contemporary appearance. The VL's 16-inch alloy wheels also fill out the wheel arches nicely. It is also a practical size.

At 4,495mm long, 1,740mm wide and 1,460mm tall, with a 2,620mm wheelbase, the Almera is compact enough for city driving without sacrificing cabin space. The trunk offers up to 474-liters. And that is one of the things I like about a sedan. You get a proper trunk rather than having to fold the rear seats every time you need to carry luggage.
Stylish interior

Inside, Nissan has done a good job of making the Almera feel more upmarket than its price suggests. The VL gets black leather seats with blue stitching, a seven-inch TFT instrument display and soft-touch dashboard trim. There is also a 60:40 split-folding rear seat, automatic air-conditioning, push-button start and cruise control.
The eight-inch touchscreen supports Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, so connecting your phone is straightforward. There are also USB ports and a six-speaker audio system.
Powertrain

Under the hood, it gets a 1.0-liter turbocharged three-cylinder engine producing 100-PS and 152-Nm. Power goes through a continuously variable transmission (CVT), while an idling-stop system helps reduce unnecessary fuel consumption when you're stationary.

On paper, it is a small engine, but on the road, it comes into its own. The turbo gives the Almera useful torque from 2,400 rpm, and the CVT keeps the engine rpms in its economical range. In traffic, this is exactly what you want.
Safety

Nissan has also made safety a significant part of the Almera package. The VL gets Blind Spot Warning, Rear Cross Traffic Alert, Lane Departure Warning, High Beam Assist, Intelligent Around View Monitor with Moving Object Detection, Intelligent Emergency Braking and Intelligent Forward Collision Warning. Both VE and VL variants also have six airbags, ABS with EBD and Brake Assist, Vehicle Dynamic Control, TPMS and ISOFIX.

Then there's NissanConnect Services. This is one of those features that sounds like a gimmick until you actually use it. Through the NissanConnect app, owners can remotely start or stop the engine, lock or unlock the doors, activate the horn and lights, locate the car, check vehicle health and receive maintenance reminders. Safety functions include automatic collision notification, SOS emergency assistance, theft alerts and customizable speed, zone and curfew alerts.
And yes, remote starting the engine also means you can get the air-conditioning going before you get into the car, which, on hot days in the Philippines, is something I would happily use every day.
Impressions and price

The Almera is easy to maneuver, the steering is light and the suspension does a respectable job of dealing with the imperfections found on Philippine roads. Once you're out on the highway, it remains composed. And while it isn't particularly sporty, it is comfortable, and very spacious. That's important for a car that will probably spend most of its life on the road and probably in traffic.

The current price for the Almera VL Turbo CVT with NissanConnect Services is ₱1,199,000. Now, it isn't the cheapest car, its running costs are a good consideration. You get a small turbocharged engine and relatively low vehicle weight which translates into less mass and less engine displacement to move around every day. When gasoline prices are high, that matters.

The Nissan Almera may not be the most fashionable choice in today's SUV-obsessed market. But sometimes the sensible choice is the one that makes the most sense every time you turn the key. And right now, the Almera makes a very good argument for the “humble” sedan.

articles.title: Regional powers seek off-ramp from Iran war, and other Middle East developments
articles.summary: Qatar and other regional powers sought an off-ramp from the war with Iran on Thursday as another tanker attack was reported in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Iranian government dismissed the Trump…

blocks.text: Qatar and other regional powers sought an off-ramp from the war with Iran on Thursday as another tanker attack was reported in the Strait of Hormuz, and the Iranian government dismissed the Trump administration's latest sanctions.

blocks.caption: Palestinians walk past a food-aid warehouse damaged in an Israeli airstrike that targeted a nearby house in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana)

blocks.text: Palestinians walk past a food-aid warehouse damaged in an Israeli airstrike that targeted a nearby house in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, Wednesday, Aug. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana)

Elsewhere in the Middle East, Israel continued its attacks on Gaza and Lebanon even as the country's strikes on Gaza drew a sharp rebuke from the top diplomat overseeing the U.S.-brokered ceasefire in the territory.
Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East. Full coverage can be found here.
Diplomatic efforts by Qatar and Pakistan
Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani was in Tehran on Thursday as part of Qatar's efforts to resolve the conflict between the United States and Iran.

Qatar's foreign ministry said in a post on X that Al Thani's meeting with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi included talks on "the efforts being made to reduce escalation," as well as a proposed plan between Iran and Oman to allow ships safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and clear the vital commercial waterway of dangerous mines.

Al Thani's office said the prime minister emphasized the "necessity of respecting the sovereignty of neighboring countries and the freedom of navigation" through the strait. He also met Thursday with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian and its parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf.

Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, underscored the longstanding ties between the two nations, noting that Iran supported Qatar during difficult times. Al Thani said Qatar has never hesitated to cooperate with Iran.
U.S. President Donald Trump told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that he has "no time schedule" to wrap up the conflict that will reach the six-month mark on Friday.
Oil tanker attacked in Strait of Hormuz
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization said Thursday that it had received a report of an oil tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz.

The monitoring agency, run by the British military, said that local authorities reported that the vessel was hit by an unknown projectile on Tuesday in the waters between Oman and Iran, causing it to catch fire.
The crew was reported to be safe and there have been no reports of environmental damage, the UKMTO said.
Oil continues to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, albeit well below prewar levels, shipping analysts say.
Ship traffic through the vital waterway increased last week compared to the prior week, with the number of oil and gas carriers up 50%, according to Lloyd's List Intelligence.

The U.S. government has claimed that up to 9 million barrels a day are flowing through the strait "over short time periods," but commodities analysts at ING bank cautioned that the figure "seems aggressive."
Other ship-tracking estimates suggest it's closer to 2 to 6 million barrels per day, ING said. Before the war, some 15 million barrels per day passed the strait.
Iran's foreign ministry criticizes US sanctions

Esmail Baghaei, Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, wrote late Wednesday in a social media post that the U.S. had made a coalition with Bahrain, calling it a country with "virtually no meaningful economic exchange with Iran."
In another social media post on Wednesday, Iran's top negotiator and parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf thanked China for rejecting the U.S. "economic D-Day" policies against Iran.
Earlier this week, Tehran had warned that it would respond harshly to expanded U.S. sanctions, including measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington.
Syria appoints former SDF leader to political position
Days after the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces announced its dissolution, Syria's interim President Ahmad al-Sharaa appointed the former SDF leader to a position as one of his advisers.

SDF commander Mazloum Abdi on Tuesday announced that the SDF had completed a merger with the Syrian army and would cease to operate as an independent force. The Kurdish-led force, which once controlled the country's northeast, lost most of its territory to a government offensive in January and then signed the deal to merge with the army.

The announcement by al-Sharaa's office of Abdi's appointment came hours after a decree from the education ministry that Kurdish classes would be taught in public and private schools "in areas where Kurdish citizens constitute a significant percentage of the population."

The inclusion of Kurdish as an official language of instruction had been one of Abdi's main demands. Questions remain about the fate of the SDF's all-female fighting units — a sensitive point in the integration talks as many of the Damascus leaders come from a conservative background and are opposed to women in combat. Discussions are underway about integrating the Women's Protection Units (YPJ) into the interior ministry as a counterterrorism force.
Israeli strikes kill 4 in Gaza
In Gaza, Israeli strikes left four people killed and several others wounded, local health officials said.

Three of the victims were killed in separate strikes in Gaza City, officials at Shifa hospital said. The fourth person was killed and others were injured in a strike on a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in southern Gaza, officials at Nasser hospital said.
Israel's military said the four strikes targeted Hamas militants.
Nickolay Mladenov, head of Trump's Board of Peace, admonished Israel during a United Nations gathering over Israel's continued attacks on Wednesday.
Israel's deputy U.N. ambassador, Noa Furman, told the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday that Israel is committed to Trump's peace plan, but that Hamas' "disarmament must come first."
Dutch diplomats removed from Gaza ceasefire efforts
Israel's foreign ministry is removing two Dutch diplomats from the Gaza ceasefire coordination center, the Dutch foreign ministry said in a statement.

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said that the decision was in response to "a series of anti-Israel measures taken by the Dutch government," including next month's implementation of a ban on the trade of Israeli products from the occupied West Bank and other areas.

Tom Berendsen, the foreign minister of the Netherlands, told The Associated Press in an email that he felt the removal of the diplomats was "unnecessary" but that his country stood by its decision "to ban products from illegal settlements."
Israeli airstrikes on Lebanon kill 1 woman
Israeli airstrikes in southern Lebanon on Thursday killed one woman and wounded six people, including a child, inside a home, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency said.
The strikes came after Israel blamed the militant Hezbollah group for firing two explosive drones.

The Israeli military said Hezbollah had fired two explosive drones at Israeli troops near the southern city of Nabatiyeh earlier Thursday, though the drones did not inflict any casualties among troops before one was shot down.
Pakistan and Kuwait reach military deal
Pakistan's military announced Thursday that it has agreed to assist Kuwait's military with training, capacity building and border management.
The Pakistani armed forces said the deal was signed by Kuwait's defense minister during a visit to the garrison city of Rawalpindi focused on bilateral defense relations and security cooperation.

Gulf states, long reliant on American protection, have been considering alternative security arrangements in the wake of the war between Iran and the U.S. In early August, Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defense pact with Pakistan and Turkey.
Pakistan said Thursday that it was also continuing diplomatic efforts with Iran, citing a recent visit to Tehran focused on reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Palawan Group of Companies launches 'Palawan for All' as it marks 41 years of serving Filipinos
articles.summary: The Palawan Group of Companies is marking its 41st anniversary with the launch of “Palawan for All,” a campaign that brings together its expanding portfolio of financial services under a single…

blocks.text: The Palawan Group of Companies is marking its 41st anniversary with the launch of “Palawan for All,” a campaign that brings together its expanding portfolio of financial services under a single commitment to make financial solutions more accessible, affordable, and relevant to Filipinos.

Unveiled during a media gathering in Makati, the campaign highlights Palawan’s evolution from its established pawning and remittance businesses into a broader financial services group offering solutions spanning digital payments, microinsurance, credit, business services, and wealth-building.

The company said the campaign recognizes the diverse financial priorities of Filipinos at different stages of life, from managing a first paycheck and sending money to family to growing a business, protecting assets, and preparing for the future.

“Today, millions of Filipinos entrust us with their hard-earned money because we have remained true to our promise of providing affordable, reliable, and accessible services. More than our growth, what makes me proud is knowing that generations of Filipinos continue to see Palawan as a partner they can trust,” said Bobby L. Castro, chairman and founder of the Palawan Group of Companies.
Combining physical reach with digital convenience
As Filipino consumers increasingly turn to digital channels for their financial needs, Palawan continues to maintain its extensive physical presence while expanding its digital services.

The company operates more than 3,800 branches nationwide, providing familiar touchpoints for its customers or “sukis.” At the same time, its PalawanPay e-wallet has grown to 23 million users, offering services such as money transfers, bill payments, QR Ph transactions, and digital pawn renewals.
Palawan describes this strategy as a “BrickTech” approach, combining the accessibility and familiarity of its physical branch network with the convenience of digital financial services.
According to Karlo M. Castro, president and CEO of the Palawan Group of Companies, the company’s expansion is driven by the changing needs of its customers.

“As our customers’ needs have changed, Palawan has continued to evolve with them. Today, we bring together different brands and services that can support Filipinos in different ways, from sending and receiving money to accessing credit, protecting their families, managing a business, and planning for the future. We want to make these financial services more understandable, convenient, and relevant to the everyday lives of Filipinos,” said Castro.

He added that the company aims to make financial services “more understandable, convenient, and relevant” to the everyday lives of Filipinos while remaining committed to its promise of “serbisyong may malasakit”: Matatag, Maaasahan, at Mapagkakatiwalaan.
Expanding beyond everyday transactions
The Palawan Group’s growing portfolio is designed to address financial needs beyond traditional remittance and pawning services.

Palawan ProtekTODO offers microinsurance designed to provide affordable financial protection, while Palawan Gold and Palawan Pawnshop Jewelry provide options for customers looking to build and preserve wealth.
For entrepreneurs and customers seeking additional financial support, Palawan for Business and Palawan Credit provide solutions intended to help them pursue their respective financial goals.

The company said these services form part of its broader effort to provide practical financial solutions as Filipinos manage expenses, send money to loved ones, protect their families, grow businesses, and prepare for the future.
Marian Rivera continues partnership with Palawan
The launch also marked the second year of actress and television personality Marian Rivera as the Palawan Group’s brand ambassador.
Rivera said she sees a strong connection between her own evolving priorities and Palawan’s expansion into a broader range of financial services.

“What I appreciate most is that Palawan has grown alongside Filipino families. I’ve seen how the brand has evolved as our lives and financial needs have changed. Before, sending money home meant going to a branch, but today, with PalawanPay, you can send money, make payments, renew your pawn, and manage everyday financial transactions anytime, anywhere—something that fits the way many of us live today,” she said.
Rivera’s continued partnership with the company is anchored on shared values of family, hard work, trust, and genuine care for Filipinos.
Building the next chapter of financial inclusion

For Bernard V. Kaibigan, Chief Marketing Officer of the Palawan Group of Companies, “Palawan for All” is ultimately about the people behind the financial transactions rather than the products themselves.

“Palawan for All brings these different services together under one promise: to be a financial partner for Filipinos through the different chapters of their lives. It is a campaign about people, not products. Every Filipino has a different financial journey, but everyone deserves a partner they can rely on, whether they are starting their first job, supporting their family, growing a business, or planning for the future,” said Kaibigan.

As it enters its next chapter, the Palawan Group said it will continue combining its nationwide physical presence with digital services to give Filipinos greater flexibility in managing their finances.

Through “Palawan for All,” the company is positioning its 41-year legacy as a foundation for its continued expansion, with the goal of remaining a trusted financial partner for Filipinos across generations.

articles.title: The REDMI Note 17 Series puts long-term reliability at the center of the smartphone experience
articles.summary: The smartphone industry is entering a new phase of ownership. As annual upgrades become less dramatic for many users, smartphones are staying in people's hands for longer. That shift is changing what…

blocks.text: The smartphone industry is entering a new phase of ownership. As annual upgrades become less dramatic for many users, smartphones are staying in people's hands for longer. That shift is changing what users expect from their devices: not simply strong performance on day one, but dependable battery life, durability and smooth everyday use over time.

For users, the ownership experience matters as much as the first impression. A phone is carried through commutes, travel, work and daily life; it needs to remain reliable after repeated charging, unexpected drops and exposure to the elements. As replacement cycles lengthen, the qualities that support long-term use are becoming increasingly important.
This raises a more meaningful question for the industry: if smartphones are becoming long-term companions rather than short-cycle upgrades, what should define a truly good smartphone experience?
Proven Over 500 Million Times

For Xiaomi, the answer has never started with specifications alone. It has always started with users. REDMI Note Series is the clearest expression of that philosophy. Through generations and more than 500 million shipments to users worldwide, REDMI Note Series has made advanced smartphone experiences more accessible while steadily raising the bar for quality in the mid-tier segment, evolving alongside users' changing needs.

Take REDMI Note, the Series' foundational model. It responded to mid-tier users' demand for large displays and a well-rounded everyday experience, breaking with market conventions at the time and establishing a durable product identity. By Redmi Note 3 Series, user feedback pointed to a desire for better build quality and longer battery life. The response was a metal body paired with a high-capacity battery. Redmi Note 7 Series sharpened the Series' focus on quality and durability. As users increasingly expected phones that could better withstand everyday drops and water exposure, while also needing stronger support when repairs were required, the Series strengthened durability and extended warranty coverage. By Redmi Note 13 Series, expectations had expanded further. Bringing IP68 water and dust resistance to the mid-tier segment, it delivered a new level of all-round reliability.

For more than a dozen generations, being "user-driven" has never been a slogan for REDMI Note Series. It is simply how the Series has been built, year after year. Generations of REDMI Note tell the same story: solving real user needs is more enduring than chasing short-term trends.

"Everything we do at REDMI is guided by two principles: premium products made accessible, premium quality across every product," says Anne Wang, REDMI Marketing Director at Xiaomi International. "Users want devices they can rely on every day and keep with confidence over time. Delivering lasting quality has always been central to REDMI Note. With the upcoming REDMI Note 17 Series, we're taking that commitment further than ever through REDMI Titan Quality. Our ambition is to build smartphones that stand the test of time and make that level of quality accessible to far more people. That's the thinking behind what we call 'Built for Years.' And this generation will also introduce the first-ever Pro Max model, bringing max design, max quality, and max experience to the REDMI Note Series."
REDMI Note 17 Series: Built for Years

Built for Years is not a single feature. It is REDMI's long-term product philosophy, bringing together R&D investment, global manufacturing capabilities and insights from generations of product evolution around one goal: building smartphones that remain dependable for years. That long-term focus has grown alongside Xiaomi's global expansion. In July 2026, Xiaomi was included in the Fortune Global 500 list for the eighth year in a row, ranking 232nd.

That philosophy matters beyond the phone itself. Under Xiaomi's Human × Car × Home smart ecosystem strategy, the smartphone serves as a high-frequency gateway to connected devices and everyday scenarios. A device designed to remain reliable over time therefore helps keep the wider experience consistent. The upcoming REDMI Note 17 Series is where that approach reaches its fullest expression. It is designed around a six-year Built for Years commitment, covering battery longevity, security patch updates and sustained smoothness, with specific coverage varying by product model and market. This focus on long-term use is not new to REDMI Note Series. As early as Redmi Note 7 in 2019, the Series extended its warranty to 18 months, well beyond the standard 12-month coverage at the time.

Now, REDMI Note 17 Series takes this approach further through TÜV SÜD certifications across three categories of smartphone durability: battery performance, drop resistance and water resistance. The tests are designed to reflect real-world usage, not just laboratory performance. Together, they form a comprehensive durability system centered on the Built for Years philosophy.

Long-term ownership begins with a battery that still feels dependable years later. One of the most common reasons people replace a smartphone is not that it has become obsolete, but that its battery no longer keeps up. Xiaomi's largest-ever battery, using industry-leading silicon-carbon technology to overcome conventional battery limitations, will be introduced to REDMI Note 17 Series to deliver exceptional battery life. The new-generation battery system is designed to address the key challenges of extended use: gradual capacity decline and safety over time. It balances daily endurance, long-term cycle life, safety and fast-charging capability, while withstanding extreme temperatures and mechanical stress including drops and pressure. Rated for 1,600 charging cycles with over 80% capacity retention, it is built to sustain six years of reliable performance under demanding daily use.

Real life rarely happens in a laboratory. It happens in the rain, on the pavement, in a backpack or on a crowded commute. A phone built for years should also endure years of everyday accidents. From accidental drops to heavy rain and prolonged water exposure, smartphones increasingly face conditions far beyond ordinary lab scenarios. Seventeen custom waterproof components and ten airtightness tests support strong water resistance across high-temperature, immersion and spray scenarios. An unexpected rainstorm, a spilled drink or an accidental drop into water is therefore less likely to interrupt the day. Certified for 3-meter drop resistance, the device is built to handle everyday incidents such as a bump against a table edge or a drop on pavement, as well as more demanding outdoor conditions. The goal is simple: reduce the risk of damage from the situations users encounter most, so the phone stays functional through years of use, not just careful handling.
Why longevity matters for mid-tier smartphones

The smartphone industry is entering a new phase. As consumers keep their devices longer, longevity is emerging as a competitive benchmark alongside performance, imaging and design — especially in the mid-tier, where a dependable all-round experience matters every day. A smartphone that lasts longer can provide a more consistent ownership experience, with less disruption from battery aging, physical damage or an earlier-than-expected replacement.

REDMI Note 17 Series is the latest expression of this philosophy, bringing together long-lasting battery, reinforced durability and long-term support in a device designed not just for the first weeks of use, but for years of ownership.

As smartphones become long-term companions rather than short-cycle upgrades, the question is no longer simply which phone has the biggest specifications today. It is which phone will still be worth relying on years from now. For consumers, that means less time worrying about battery aging, unexpected repairs or replacing a phone sooner than expected — and more time simply using it. REDMI believes the answer lies in building smartphones designed to remain reliable for years. That belief is what Built for Years stands for.

articles.title: People from more than 30 countries are missing after the flash floods in Nepal and China
articles.summary: Catastrophic flash floods in a border area of China and Nepal have killed at least 359 people and left more than 1,400 people missing as of Thursday. Many were foreigners in the area for trekking,…

blocks.text: Catastrophic flash floods in a border area of China and Nepal have killed at least 359 people and left more than 1,400 people missing as of Thursday. Many were foreigners in the area for trekking, guided tours or a pilgrimage to a sacred Hindu site.

blocks.caption: People walk past damage in the aftermath of flash floods in Devighat in the Nuwakot district in Nepal, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

blocks.text: People walk past damage in the aftermath of flash floods in Devighat in the Nuwakot district in Nepal, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha)

The number of missing from Wednesday's disaster may vary across agencies because of differences in how they collected data, when it was reported and how it was verified, as well as gaps in coordination between those assembling data and those conducting rescue efforts in the affected area.
A look at how multiple countries have been affected:
Nepal

Nepal's disaster management authority said the death toll has risen to 359, with 910 people, including 517 foreign nationals, still missing. The authority added that 50 foreigners have been rescued by air so far.

Local reports cited the National Emergency Operation Center as saying Thursday the missing included 113 Nepali tourists, 85 security personnel from the army and police as well as 161 residents from the Rasuwa district and one from the Nuwakot district.

articles.title: Trump signs order renaming Lake Ontario as 'Lake America' in the United States
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as "Lake America" in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada. The Republican…

blocks.text: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said Thursday he is renaming Lake Ontario to be known as "Lake America" in the United States as he escalates his trade war with Canada.

blocks.caption: President Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order in the Oval Office of the White House, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

blocks.text: President Donald Trump holds up a signed executive order in the Oval Office of the White House, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Manuel Balce Ceneta)

The Republican president signed an executive order directing the Interior Department to update the lake's name in the U.S. geographic naming service. Trump cannot force Canada to follow along, however.

Trump has been floating the idea of the name change in recent days as the U.S. announced it was imposing 50% tariffs on $20 billion worth of Canadian goods over the weekend after talks between the countries broke down. Trump has been needling America's northern neighbor since he returned to the White House last year, suggesting the ally with whom the U.S. once had warm relations should instead be absorbed as the 51st state.
Canada responded to Trump's import taxes this week by imposing retaliatory tariffs on $20 billion worth of American goods, including steel, dairy products, appliances and farm equipment.

Trump, who signed the order as he was sitting at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office, had a large sign behind him propped on a stand with a map of the Great Lakes. Over Lake Ontario, in big red letters, the map read "Lake America."
On the other side of the president was another map with the words, "MAKING THE GREAT LAKES EVEN GREATER."
Trump said as he was signing the order that he'd "notified all of the various people that we have to notify. So, we've done everything that you have to do."
"And this is official, effective immediately," he added.
But the executive order Trump signed shows that the changes are supposed to be made within 30 days.
Canadian officials dismissed Trump's move.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, invoking the lake's Indigenous roots and noting that the name predates both Canadian Confederation and the U.S. Declaration of Independence.
"Canadians also know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario — then, now and always," he wrote.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has traded insults with Trump, said on X: "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said, "We're into some real foolishness now. It's Lake Ontario, buddy."

The lake is one of multiple Great Lakes that the U.S. and Canada share borders along. New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat whose state shares a border on the lake, wrote on X in response to the White House's announcement that, "New York won't be calling it that."
There is no single international body that determines names of international bodies of water and Trump has wide latitude over how the U.S. government recognizes geographic places and landmarks.
The name Lake Ontario comes from the Huron Indigenous people's word "oniatarí:io," which means "lake of shining waters." The province of Ontario, founded in 1867, took its name from the lake.
Trump said that while his action was not meant to send any particular geopolitical message, "Canada's been ripping us off for a long time" on trade and military issues.
"They wanted to be treated like a state and they're not a state," the president said. "We just can't do that anymore."
"We love the people of Canada," Trump added. "I don't think their representatives do, an appropriate job. Maybe they'll change. I really don't know. It doesn't make much difference."
The move is reminiscent of his move last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America."
Trump scribbled his name with a Sharpie pen on the executive order, then held it up for the cameras, offering, "And we filed all the necessary papers, documents, everything else."
He also suggested his push to rename bodies of water may not be finished.

"So, if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake. Now, all we need is an ocean," Trump said. "So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and/or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them."

articles.title: As super El Nino strengthens, study suggests that climate change is intensifying El Ninos
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — A new study suggests that El Ninos — the natural climatic chaos agent that pops up periodically and spikes global temperatures — are getting stronger because of human-caused climate…

blocks.text: FILE - A woman uses a fan to cool off while riding a bus on a hot day in Bucharest, Romania, Aug. 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Vadim Ghirda)

WASHINGTON (AP) — A new study suggests that El Ninos — the natural climatic chaos agent that pops up periodically and spikes global temperatures — are getting stronger because of human-caused climate change.

El Ninos are more than 36% stronger than they were before the industrial age began in the mid 1800s, with a 16% jump in just the last 40 years showing that the increase is accelerating, according to a study in Thursday's journal Science. The findings come as a strong El Nino that formed a couple months ago is forecast to be the biggest on record in coming months. El Ninos, which are a temporary warming of parts of the equatorial Pacific, warp weather worldwide and increase extreme events, including heat waves, floods in some places and droughts in others. They can cost trillions in damage.

"That's important because strong El Ninos have much stronger impacts on climate hazards and extremes worldwide. When we set out to answer the question of why this might be happening, we set our data up against a record of global temperature, and we found that the increase in El Nino's strength closely parallels the rise in global temperature that is due to human causes such as the burning of fossil fuels," said study lead author Julia Cole, a paleoclimate scientist at the University of Michigan.
Her study looks back at El Ninos going back 900 years or so.
Aggravating already nasty El Ninos

"El Nino is the most violent aspect of climate variability worldwide, with effects ranging from local fisheries collapse, to widespread coral die-offs to severe droughts and food shortages around the world," said Dalhousie University marine scientist Boris Worm, who wasn't part of the study.

Worm quoted the late climate scientist Wallace Broecker who warned "the climate system is an angry beast and we are poking it with sticks." And then Worm added: "Human emissions are the stick and El Nino is of the 'angry' outbursts that can be so threatening to our collective safety."

An El Nino's strength is determined by measuring water temperature in a region of the central Pacific around the equator and comparing a three-month average to normal. If it's 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than normal, it's becomes an El Nino. The top of the scale is 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and is called "very strong." The most recent weekly El Nino figure is at 2.7 degrees (4.9 degrees Fahrenheit) and is expected to keep growing for another two to four months, according to Columbia University's El Nino tracker.

Scientists have long theorized that as the world warms, El Ninos would get stronger because they are based on ocean temperature differences compared to average. But observational records only goes back about 75 years, so scientists have previously said the data is too spotty for a trend. So scientists have looked for clues that indicate an El Nino without measuring water temperatures directly. Scientists, for example, have looked back at historical records of changes in weather around the world and figured out past El Ninos — such as the super-sized one in 1877 — due to the changes they cause across the globe.
Using coral fossils to study temperature

Cole's team took a novel approach by looking at at what happened to coral over the centuries to act as "a time machine to look into the past," she said. Cole said measurements of the ratio of calcium and strontium in coral skeletons and of different oxygen isotopes create two independent readings of the seawater in which the coral formed. Another measurement of uranium and thorium tell when those skeletons were formed.

Cole looked at 29 coral fossils in the Galapagos Islands — 14 from before the industrial era, 14 after the modern era began and one more from about the time the industrial era was starting up. The oldest was from around year 1100.

The temperatures she derived from the fossils over more than 900 years are patchy, with gaps, but when charted it, she said it looks like a hockey stick, the same description used for a 1990s landmark study of past global temperatures.
She and other scientists say it's only going to get worse.

"It raises the specter of a future where larger El Niño and La Niña events are dialing up the pace and severity of weather and climate extremes.," said Kim Cobb, a coral and climate scientist at Brown University, who wasn't part of the study.
Outside scientists split on the research
Outside scientists are split on the research with some hailing it as important and trustworthy and others saying they don't buy it because it clashes with some recent observations.

"Corals are the gold standard for El Niño reconstruction, and this brings a goldmine of new material to the table," Cobb said. "We can either wait many many decades for the instrumental record to get long enough to detect a shift in El Niño properties, or we can use centuries of El Niño reconstructions provided by paleoclimate records. Taken together, the paleoclimate data that we have, from across the Pacific, is fairly consistent in pointing to an intensification of El Niño's with global warming."

Both University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann — originator of the temperature hockey stick — and University of North Carolina marine scientist John Bruno said that the coral data conflicts with recent observations of water temperature in the Galapagos. Data shows "a substantial decline in recent decades" of El Nino related variations near the Galapagos during the time greenhouse gases increased temperatures the most, Mann said.
What's being reflected by the coral is not a change in El Nino as much as the warming from greenhouse gases, Bruno said.

Cole said the huge 1997-1998 El Nino and then small ones until 2023-24 created a situation where it seems like El Nino's aren't strengthening because measurements are based on a 20-year time period and there were a few years that fell between super El Ninos that skewed data. She said El Nino varies in strength so much and that up-and-down nature doesn't go away just because it is responding to warmer conditions.
But the scientists all agreed that climate change is a problem, with or without El Nino worsening.
"It's important to point to this as one more reason why we need to get off fossil fuels," Cole said. "There isn't a magic bullet that's going to slow El Ninos down."

Qatar’s prime minister visited Tehran on Thursday, August 27, in an effort to revive stalled diplomacy six months into the war, as US President Donald Trump said Washington was not currently talking to Iran.

“We don’t want to speak to them. We’re not looking to meet or anything,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office after the White House said a US economic campaign against Tehran would continue until Iran decides to negotiate meaningfully.

Major combat operations have been paused for weeks but there has been little progress toward a wider peace agreement or reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping route. Six months after US and Israeli forces attacked Iran, killing its supreme leader and maiming his son and successor, the Iranian government is under economic siege, but it still holds power and has shown little urgency to negotiate.

Trump, facing political pressure at home over higher energy prices ahead of November congressional elections, has opted to focus on economic sanctions, but aggressively enforcing them would require taking measures against Iranian trade partners such as China and India.

In Tehran, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani urged a return to diplomacy during talks with Iran’s top negotiator Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf on Thursday, Qatar’s foreign ministry said.

Iran in turn called on regional neighbors to prevent the US from using their territory to carry out military or economic attacks on Iran, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on his Telegram account.

Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told the Qatari prime minister that Tehran would strike US military and economic interests if Washington engaged in “mischief” against Iran, Iranian media reported.

Rezaei said the United States must take steps to meet Iran’s conditions before Tehran moved to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Those conditions include an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions.
“We do not trust the United States; it has repeatedly betrayed diplomacy and negotiations,” Rezaei said.

A June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran collapsed in part over the future of the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman through which about a fifth of global energy supplies passed before the war.
Iran has sought to exert control over the strait and charge fees to ships it authorizes, while Washington insists it should remain an open international waterway.

Al Thani said on X that he stressed the importance of freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. He and the Iranian foreign minister also discussed a proposal to establish a temporary joint Iranian-Omani shipping corridor through the strait and a joint project to clear mines, Qatar’s foreign ministry said.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that Iran and Oman had agreed in principle on administering traffic in the strait and sharing revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement.

Iran is preparing a list of conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz after mediators asked Tehran to set them out, Rezaei said. Ships would use a designated central channel if the US met Iran’s conditions, he said through an interpreter in an Al Manar TV interview.
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said on Thursday that Trump “continues to retain all options on the table” with regard to Iran.
“We’ve had Operation Epic Fury to destroy their military. Now we have Operation Economic Outcast to destroy their economy,” Leavitt said in an interview with Fox News.
“No negotiations are happening right now, and this will continue until the president feels that maybe they come to the table in a meaningful way,” she said. “We have not seen that yet.”
Tehran has lived under various forms of US sanctions since the Islamic revolution in 1979.
Despite suffering heavy military losses, Iran retains enough missile and drone capability to strike Gulf states that host US forces and disrupt shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Maritime Organization has reported 70 incidents in the strait since February 28 that have killed 19 seafarers.

Thousands of others have died, mostly in Iran and Lebanon, since the US and Israel attacked Iran with the stated goals of denying Iran a nuclear weapon, helping Iranians topple their government, and destroying Tehran’s missile program. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Congo begins vaccinations to fight the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history
articles.summary: KISANGANI, Congo (AP) — Congo on Thursday began vaccinating people against Ebola as health authorities work to slow the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history. Health workers and other…

blocks.text: KISANGANI, Congo (AP) — Congo on Thursday began vaccinating people against Ebola as health authorities work to slow the fastest-growing outbreak of the disease in history.

blocks.caption: Congo’s Health Minister Roger Kamba administers an Ebola vaccine to a health care worker in Kisangani, Congo, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Samy Kamanga)

blocks.text: Congo’s Health Minister Roger Kamba administers an Ebola vaccine to a health care worker in Kisangani, Congo, Thursday, Aug. 27, 2026. (AP Photo/Samy Kamanga)

Health workers and other frontline workers in the Ebola response are being prioritized to receive the Ervebo vaccine that was effective in past Ebola outbreaks caused by a different, more common type. Clinical trials are going on to find a licensed vaccine for the current outbreak.

"We have decided to use the Ervebo vaccine to protect first those who are on the front line," Health Minister Roger Kamba said at the launch of the vaccination campaign in Kisangani, the capital of Tshopo, which is one of the six provinces affected by Ebola in the east.

As of Tuesday, the country had recorded 5,713 confirmed cases, including 2,744 deaths, according to government figures. It is concentrated in Ituri province and is known to be the deadliest of all past 17 Ebola outbreaks in the country.

The outbreak is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fueled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people, primarily in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
More than 50,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine have been received, according to Congo's state news agency.
The World Health Organization said last week that 70,000 doses of Ervebo had been approved for use in Congo.

About 50,000 doses are intended for frontline and health workers, while 20,000 doses will be used in a clinical trial to study whether the vaccine protects against Bundibugyo virus, which is causing the current outbreak and has no licensed vaccine nor treatment.

The vaccine is being used under a compassionate-use program, which allows a medical product to be used in a serious disease situation even though it has not been specifically approved for that particular use.

Health authorities said Ervebo could offer some protection against the Bundibugyo virus because the two viruses are related. But whether the vaccine can actually prevent illness in people infected with Bundibugyo Ebola is still being studied.
Placide Mbala Kingebeni, Africa CDC's director for research, clinical trials and innovation, said data will be collected during the vaccination campaign to measure how well the vaccine works.
The campaign is expected to cover 14 health zones in Tshopo, Bas-Uele and Haut-Uele provinces.
Kamba strongly encouraged health workers to get vaccinated, saying the vaccine could protect them from the disease and help prevent them from carrying the virus into their communities.

articles.byline: Ian Norman E. Dato, Undersecretary of the Department of Justice

blocks.text: This August, as the country celebrates Buwan ng Wikang Pambansa, the Philippine Trial Lawyers Association (PTLA) has once again urged the Supreme Court to allow the use of Filipino in all court proceedings nationwide. The call draws attention to a gap that has long existed between the language of our laws and the people they are meant to serve.

For many Filipinos, the courtroom can feel like a place where justice is spoken in a foreign tongue. When court proceedings are difficult to understand, people are often left to rely on their lawyers to explain what is happening to their own lives, families, and freedoms. Justice cannot feel fully accessible when the language in which it is delivered does not feel like one’s own.

The push for a more linguistically inclusive judiciary is rooted in our highest law. The 1987 Constitution recognizes Filipino as the national language and directs the government to develop and use it as a medium of official communication. More importantly, the Bill of Rights guarantees every accused person the right to be informed of the nature and cause of the accusation against them. That right is difficult to fully realize if the explanation is delivered in a language the accused does not truly understand. It is not enough for the words to be translated; they must be naiintindihan.

The Judiciary has recently shown that it is ready to take steps in this direction. In July 2026, the Supreme Court released a landmark 26-page decision in a statutory rape case written entirely in Filipino. Penned by Justice Maria Filomena Singh, the ruling emphasized language as a bridge to justice, bringing judicial reasoning closer to the public. It followed the May 2026 decision in Velarde v. Court of Tax Appeals, also written in Filipino, signaling the Judiciary’s continuing efforts toward its Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovation.

We have also seen progress in making proceedings more inclusive. Effective December 15, 2025, the Supreme Court approved the Rules on Filipino Sign Language (FSL) Interpreting in the Judiciary, which requires courts to appoint accredited FSL interpreters in cases involving Deaf Filipinos. The measure recognizes a simple principle: the pursuit of hustisya should never be limited by a person’s ability to hear or communicate in the language used by the court.

Using Filipino in court can also improve the quality of evidence. Witnesses can describe what they saw, heard, or experienced more naturally and accurately in a language they are comfortable speaking, without first translating their thoughts into English. Filipino documents are likewise already accepted under the Rules of Court without requiring a separate translation.

But making the courts more accessible does not mean pretending the transition will be easy. Legal concepts such as “preponderance of evidence” or the specific elements of estafa carry precise meanings shaped by English and Spanish legal history. Translating them requires more than finding simpler words; it requires continuing to develop Filipino as a language capable of expressing complex legal ideas accurately.

There is also our linguistic diversity. The Philippines has more than 170 languages. In the Visayas and Mindanao, an overly Tagalog-centric Filipino could create another barrier for people more comfortable with Cebuano, Ilocano, or other local languages. Accessibility should not mean replacing one unfamiliar language with another.

The answer, therefore, is not to discard English, but to use both languages wisely—much like how Filipinos actually communicate every day. The current impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte shows how moving naturally between English and Filipino can help both proceedings and the public better follow what is happening.

Ultimately, this is not simply a question of which language belongs in the courtroom. It is a question of whether people can understand the law that governs their lives, the charges brought against them, and the decisions that affect their freedom.

If the law is for the people, then its language must reach them, too. By bringing the language of the courtroom closer to the language of our kababayans, we move closer to the Constitution’s vision of a just and humane society—one where Filipinos do not merely receive justice, but can understand it when it speaks.

(Ian Norman E. Dato is the Department of Justice (DOJ) Undersecretary designated for the National Prosecution Service. The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author in his personal capacity and do not necessarily represent the official views or position of the DOJ.)

items: Nepal and China have issued warnings about potential flooding risks due to two lakes threatening to burst in the Himalayas, following a catastrophic flood that has already killed at least 362 people and left nearly 1,000 missing.

Nepal's disaster authority has cautioned residents and rescuers to stay away from river banks and risky areas as a lake formed by debris is rising, while China anticipates a significant flow of water into a dammed lake, increasing the risk of a breach.
