TRISHULI, Nepal – Nepal and China both warned on Thursday, August 27, of fresh risks of flooding in the Himalayas as two lakes that have developed on either side of their border threaten to burst in a region still grappling with this week’s catastrophic flood.

Search and rescue operations are still underway in the debris-strewn valleys and hillsides, with nearly 1,000 people still missing after Wednesday’s flood struck the border regions of Nepal and China’s Tibet, killing at least 362 people.
Both countries have blamed the flood on a glacier collapse that pushed rock, ice, mud and debris into river systems in the mountains.

blocks.caption: Filipino among missing in Nepal after deadly flash floods

blocks.text: Nepal’s disaster authority issued a notice on Thursday warning that a lake formed by debris blocking a river at the flood site is rising and at risk of bursting.

“Residents of the lower banks… passengers, rescuers engaged in rescue operations, and all concerned are requested to exercise special caution and stay in safe places away from the river banks and risky areas,” the authority said.

China warned that 3 million cubic meters of water — the equivalent of about 1,200 Olympic swimming pools — are expected to flow into an already dammed lake on its side of the border over the next three days, creating a high risk of a breach, with peak flow expected around September 1.
The formation of a barrier lake was captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team on Thursday, state broadcaster CGTN reported.

The footage showed masses of brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet. The water had already submerged bushes and trees and appeared to push against a barrier of debris and stones.More rain expected
Rainfall forecast over the coming week will exacerbate the threat, Chinese state media said, citing the Chinese water resources ministry.
“The volume of water is continuing to increase, and so is the risk,” Zhu Jinfeng, a researcher at the water resources ministry’s hydrology department, told state broadcaster CCTV.
Heeding the warning, some rescue workers in Nepal began moving towards higher ground on Thursday.
Among them was Pawan Koirala, who began moving away from the river bed along with his team of 13 after the warning was issued.
“We are here for rescue and don’t want to be near the danger zone,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.summary: NEW YORK (AP) — Peter Cullen, a prolific voice actor who enlivened scores of TV series, specials and movies, including Optimus Prime in the syndicated 1984 series “Transformers” and Eeyore in the…

blocks.text: NEW YORK (AP) — Peter Cullen, a prolific voice actor who enlivened scores of TV series, specials and movies, including Optimus Prime in the syndicated 1984 series “Transformers” and Eeyore in the Winnie the Pooh cartoon franchise, has died. He was 85.

His agent, Kevin Motley, said Cullen died Wednesday at his home in Los Angeles. “His family asks that you honor his remarkable legacy by serving your communities and leading others with compassion, integrity, and loyalty and always remember ‘be strong enough to be gentle,’” said a family statement.

Cullen’s career spanned from being an announcer at the groundbreaking late-1960s comedy and variety series “The Smothers Brothers Comedy Hour” and joining comedy sketches for Sonny & Cher to voice acting in “The Smurfs” and multiple G.I. Joe iterations. But he struck a nerve as Optimus Prime.
When Cullen read about the heroic Autobot leader that turned into a red cabover semitrailer, he thought about his older brother, who had served as a U.S. Marine in the Vietnam War.

“He was my hero, and he certainly was the mainstay behind the character,” Cullen said. “I just did an impression of Larry, and he’s still alive in my mind today because every time I do Prime, there’s my brother Larry.”
Cullen received a lifetime achievement award at the Children’s & Family Emmy Awards in 2023 and was nominated for a Daytime Emmy for voicing Optimus Prime in 2011.

articles.title: Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America
articles.summary: Trump's order comes after the trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has signed an executive order seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America.

The move comes after trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed late last week, and the US imposed new 50% tariffs on $20bn (C$28bn) worth of Canadian goods. Canada will implement "dollar for dollar" counter tariffs next month.
Trump has repeatedly posted threats about renaming the lake, one of the five Great Lakes that straddle both countries, on social media amid the trade dispute.
He said on Thursday the move was "official, effective immediately" and that his administration has "filed all the necessary papers, documents" to make the change.

Text of the executive order says it gives the US Department of the Interior 30 days to update the name change with the Geographic Names Information Service - the official repository of domestic geographic names in the US.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney noted the name Lake Ontario can be traced back more than 400 years, adding in a social media post on Thursday that preceded the formation of the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence.

"We know that the United States is changing. Their trade relations, their foreign policy, their national monuments, their hydronyms," he wrote. "Canadian women and men also know that things must be called by their name, and this lake is called Lake Ontario – today and forever."

When Trump took the White House in 2025, he signed a similar order that changed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. Mexico has rejected the name change, arguing a single country cannot rename a shared body of international water.
It also led to a legal dispute between Mexico and tech giant Google, which renamed the gulf in its maps application. , external
In that case, Google Maps users in the US see "Gulf of America", while those in Mexico see the "Gulf of Mexico". Those in other countries see the "Gulf of Mexico (Gulf of America)".

The White House at the time also blocked Associated Press reporters from presidential events over the news agency's refusal to adopt the name "Gulf of America" in its coverage. The AP sued the Trump administration in response, and that legal battle is ongoing.

There is no universally recognised international body setting the names of international waters. While the US president has broad discretion over how his country officially recognises landmarks, other countries do not have to follow.
Canada does not have to recognise name changes made by other countries and officials there have dismissed the idea.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford wrote on social media, "It's Lake Ontario to Canadians and the rest of the world. Now and forever."
Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston agreed, saying "We're into some real foolishness now. It's Lake Ontario, buddy."
"We'll always call it Lake Ontario," said Industry Minister Melanie Joly on Tuesday.

The names of four of the Great Lakes - Ontario, Huron, Michigan and Erie - originate from indigenous words. Lake Superior was named after an anglicised French word. Lake Ontario, the smallest of the Great Lakes, borders both the Canadian province and the US state of New York.
As he signed the order on Thursday in the Oval Office, Trump said it wasn't a direct message to Canada, but that America's northern neighbour "has been ripping us off for a long time on trade".
Trump said he'd been thinking about renaming the lake "for a long time".
"So if you think about it, we have a gulf and we have a lake," Trump said.
"Now, all we need is an ocean. So maybe we'll have to change the name of the Atlantic and or the Pacific. Maybe we'll change them both."

The name change request comes amid a trade dispute that has seen US-Canada relations fall to new lows, with insults thrown back-and-forth between the Trump administration and Canadian officials over the past week.
There was a hint on Thursday that there was room for a return to the negotiating table sometime in the future.

Canadian US trade minister, Dominic LeBlanc, said in a post on X that the US had withdrawn some of its demands around labelling requirements in French "and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future US trade actions".
"We look forward to further constructive US clarifications on their other positions, which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade agreement that respects Canadian sovereignty".
Trade talks collapsed at the last minute late on Friday night, with both sides accusing the other of demanding last-minute changes to a tentative deal.

Democratic lawmaker Debbie Dingell of Michigan, the US state that borders four of the five Great Lakes, said that she would introduce a bill in Congress to nullify the name change, calling Trump's order "idiotic".
She wrote, "The Great Lakes are a shared treasure that generations of Americans and Canadians have worked together to protect".

Other Democratic lawmakers in the US also criticised the order on social media, calling for the Trump administration to get back to negotiating on a trade deal. Some mocked Trump's idea and posted their own ideas to change the names of other landmarks.

Wisconsin's governor joked, "I just renamed Lake Michigan Lake Wisconsin," in a social media post with a video of himself signing a napkin on one of the Great Lakes. "See, I can sign napkins that say things, too," he added.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul said her state, the sole US state bordering Lake Ontario, "won't be calling it" Lake America.
Meanwhile, Trump's Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum applauded the move, writing, "We're on it, Mr. President!"

"The places and waters that border our nation and support our economy should reflect the greatness of the United States," he said, adding that the US Geological Survey "maps our country for the world to see, and we are PROUD to implement your Executive Order to rename LAKE AMERICA".

articles.title: What we know about deadly Nepal-Tibet floods
articles.summary: Hundreds have died or are missing in Wednesday's flooding and landslides on the border of Nepal and Tibet.

blocks.text: Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border
ByOlivia Ireland and Henry Moore
Massive landslides and flash floods on the Nepal-Tibet border have caused widespread damage and left hundreds dead or missing.
Search and rescue operations are continuing after Wednesday's disaster. Chinese state media has said there are significant casualties, while Nepalese officials describe "huge scale loss".
There are risks of more floods: a lake of rising water has formed at a site along the China-Nepal border - prompting fears it could burst its banks.
Here is what we know so far.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on Wednesday

blocks.text: Image source, Nepal Army via EPA
Military teams were brought in to help with rescue and evacuation following the flooding on Wednesday
What caused the deadly landslide?
Initial reports of an earthquake on the Nepal-Tibet border led many to believe that a tremor had caused a landslide, which in turn caused the devastating flood.
However, the US Geological Survey has clarified that the disaster was caused by a "glacial collapse", which is when a glacier or part of a glacier disintegrates.
The impact of the collapsed glacier hitting the bottom of a valley was so powerful that it registered a magnitude of 5.2, according to USGS data and scientists who have analysed the event.
Debris flow from the collapse "caused subsequent catastrophic impacts downstream" the USGS said.

blocks.caption: Map showing the path of floodwaters along the Lende Khola, Bhote Koshi and  Trishuli rivers in northern Nepal after a glacier collapse near the Tibet border. The collapse sent ice and rock debris into the river, triggering flooding that destroyed a border checkpoint and continued downstream past…

blocks.text: Climate change is known to be driving faster glacier melt in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region and, as rescue efforts continue, scientists are trying to piece together the exact order of events.
Simon Cook, senior lecturer in energy environment and security at the University of Dundee who specialises in glaciology, said "climate change could have an impact".
Cook said his team had detected that the lower part of a glacier in Nepal near the Langtang Lirung peak - which is approximately 15km (9 miles) west of the site of the floods - had collapsed.
He estimated that the glacier collapsed in a north-westerly direction and then travelled westwards downstream.
He told the BBC "permafrost is partially holding some mountainsides together, this permafrost is warming and thawing and degrading so you are going to get more landslides".
Mike Searle, professor of Earth sciences at Oxford University, said the glacier could have collapsed "hours or days" before the flooding hit Nepal and Tibet.
He told the BBC: "I think the sheer wave of debris suggests there was a landslide first, the water built up, (which) dammed the river, and then it burst in one huge great flood."
One possibility is that water from rainfall or melting ice may have destabilised the ground or ice, triggering a chain reaction.

Scientist will be looking at satellite images of exactly where the landslide occurred, whether any glacial lakes suddenly drained, and where the river might have become blocked, as well as data on recent rainfall.

A deluge of material careered towards northern Nepalese towns, including areas popular with mountaineering tourists and pilgrims. The border is around 40 miles (64.4km) north of Nepal's capital city Kathmandu.
Footage showed a wall of mud and rock sweeping away buildings, roads and vehicles, as people fled the fast-moving wave of material in the Nuwakot region.
In one video, a towering wall of water and mud was seen rushing down a gorge along the Trishuli River and enveloping the Rasuvagadhi Border check point, a multi-storey building.
Severe flooding has been reported along the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers.
Deaths have also been reported in villages on the Tibetan side of the border.
The International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIDMOD) has warned secondary flooding could occur in the coming days as a result of the debris that washed into the river systems.

In a report, the ICIDMOD said they are in the process of assessing whether the Trishuli River has been temporarily blocked in narrow sections. If it has been blocked, it is at risk of forming a landslide dam - and a second flooding event.
Authorities and scientists are continuing to evaluate the size, location and stability of any potential blockages.
Watch: BBC Nepali's Shreejana Shrestha is at a hospital in Kathmandu, where some survivors are being flown in by helicopter
How many people are dead and missing?
The number of people killed or missing is still becoming clear.
Nepali police say at least 389 people have died. Among those killed, 64 were found in downstream areas in the Chitwan district while another 26 were found in Nawalparasi East.

In its latest update on Thursday evening, Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said 910 people were still missing. This included 517 foreign citizens, 44 members of the Nepal Army and 28 Nepal police officers.
Meanwhile, China's state broadcaster CCTV said on Thursday that the number of people missing in the mudslide disaster in Tibet's Gyirong county had risen to 558.
Among these are 260 foreign nationals, CCTV said, adding that the death toll remained at three.
The Nepal Tourism Board said on Thursday that 644 tourists were still missing, 33 of which were UK nationals, including a 13-year-old girl and 14-year-old boy.
It is not clear if any of the missing in the Nepali and Chinese figures have been counted twice.
The border at Gyirong is the main crossing point for tourists and traffic between China and Nepal.

blocks.caption: Police officers carrying an elderly woman who survived the flash flood at Trishuli in Nuwakot district of Nepal

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
How are governments responding?
Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah said "the entire nation has been left shocked and deeply distressed" and that officials would coordinate with China on the response.
China's President Xi Jinping urged an "all-out" search effort, and promised stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary impacts.
In neighbouring India, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said his government was "prepared to provide Nepal with all possible types of humanitarian assistance".

UN Secretary General António Guterres says he is "saddened by the severe flooding", adding that UN teams and partners are mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support the government-led response.
The US has promised $500,000 (£367,982) in aid which will be used to cover emergency shelter, water, sanitation and other relief items for communities affected by the floods.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the UK has offered £5m to help the Nepalese government and will do "everything we can" to support British nationals in Nepal.
Aerial footage shows flash flood on Nepal-Tibet border
What countries are the missing tourists from?
Tourists from all over the world come to Nepal for its mountains and sacred sites. Official figures suggested at least 291 foreigners are among the missing, including:

China - The Chinese foreign ministry says nearly 100 Chinese nationals are missing in Nepal

Ukraine - Ukraine's foreign ministry says 53 Ukrainian nationals are missing
Malaysia - 51 Malaysians travelling with Fishtail Tours and Travels are missing in the floods, officials say
Australia - Australia's foreign minister says 39 Australians are among the missing and there's an "unfortunate possibility" the number will rise
UK - Nepal's police say 33 British nationals are missing
Canada - a tourism board spokesman in Nepal says 24 Canadians are reported missing

The CoconutPhilippines Trade Fair enters its final weekend, showcasing Filipino coconut products and 300 MSMEs before the event wraps up Sunday
The humble coconut has long been part of the Filipino table, but there is much more to the fruit than gata, buko juice, and the other familiar staples.
That broader potential is what the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) is putting in the spotlight through the DTI–Bagong Pilipinas CoconutPhilippines Trade Fair, which ends this weekend.

The trade fair, which opened Aug. 26, brings together 300 micro, small, and medium enterprises working to develop products and find new markets for Philippine coconut products. For visitors, it offers a chance to discover what local businesses are creating from an ingredient that has long been part of everyday Filipino life.

There is good reason for the industry to be looking beyond the familiar. Philippine coconut exports rose 34.4 percent in 2025, reaching $3.6 billion, with the sector accounting for nearly half of the country’s total agro-based exports. It also supports 2.8 million Filipino farmers.
For DTI Secretary Ma. Cristina A. Roque, the opportunity lies not simply in harvesting coconuts, but in developing products that can create greater value for the people and communities behind them.

“The value of our coconut industry lies not only in what we harvest, but in what we create from it. We must maximize its potential by producing competitive, high-value products that generate lasting income for our farmers and local communities,” she said during the fair’s opening day.

The DTI is working to connect these enterprises with international buyers through export promotion, business-matching activities, outbound trade missions, and the Philippine Trade and Investment Centers’ global network.

There is also a wider push to open international markets for Philippine agricultural products. Cristina cited sustained overseas demand for bananas, pineapples, calamansi, and ube, while Philippine coconut exporters can also benefit from the country’s expanding network of free trade agreements, including the recently concluded Philippines-Chile FTA negotiations and ongoing discussions with the European Union and Canada.

For Filipino consumers, however, the most immediate reason to visit is simpler: there is only this weekend left to explore the fair. The CoconutPhilippines Trade Fair runs through Aug. 30, bringing together the participating enterprises and their products for those curious to see how a familiar Filipino crop is finding new expressions and new markets.

As Cristina put it: “The world already knows the exceptional quality of Philippine coconut products. Now, we must create more Filipino success stories that will bring better lives to our farmers and uplift communities nationwide.”
The fair runs through Sunday, Aug. 30, at the SMX Convention Center Manila in Pasay City.

The crisis has worsened since June, ⁠when students were released ⁠early from school for the summer ‌break as transportation and electricity faltered amid stiffened sanctions by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump.
Washington has since imposed more sanctions on a wide range of Cuban officials, accusing them of anti-American activities, as ⁠it seeks to intensify pressure on Cuba's communist leaders.
Havana says the U.S. is trying to damage its economy and prevent it providing basic services.
Education system a point of pride

Cuba has long touted ‌its free and universal state-provided education as one of its greatest achievements. But severe shortages, aggravated by the U.S. sanctions, have led many to question the viability of the model.

blocks.text: Teacher coverage at the island's schools ​has fallen to 73 per cent, according to official statistics. Many have emigrated or sought better-paying work.
Trujillo said the sector ⁠would hire university students, professionals from other sectors and call back retirees, plus offer ⁠additional compensation, to keep schools afloat.
Havana province, among the most critical ⁠in ⁠terms of staffing shortages, will receive ​about 3,000 teachers from provinces in eastern Cuba where schools are better staffed.

blocks.text: Shortages have ​also hit the ⁠distribution of school uniforms, with official garments available to meet only 12 per cent of the demand for primary school children due to ongoing blackouts at the factories where the uniforms are produced.
The minister urged schools to be flexible and welcome students in "comfortable clothes" and ⁠their traditional red neckerchiefs.

U.S. President Donald Trump's trade ambassador's recent comments about Canada's auto industry suggest the level at which it's integrated throughout North America could remain a major sticking point if talks do resume.

blocks.text: U.S. President Donald Trump's trade ambassador's recent comments about Canada's auto industry suggest the level at which it's integrated throughout North America could remain a major sticking point if talks do resume.
Trump and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have repeatedly said that the administration wants Canadian auto manufacturing jobs to move south of the border.
In a Canadian exclusive interview with CBC News, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer was asked about the future of the U.S. and Canada's integrated auto sector.
"We have a big gap in our manufacturing employment here, and autos is a big part of that," Greer told CBC News chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton on Wednesday.
WATCH | USTR blames Canada for failed trade talks:
U.S. trade rep disputes why talks fell apart | Canadian exclusive

"I don't think this is any secret — we believe that the process of globalization for the United States, of integrating with other economies — even our close neighbours with whom, you know, we trade a lot — we think that has had some negative effects, especially in places like Michigan and Ohio and Pennsylvania and Wisconsin," he said.
When asked if the goal of the Trump administration is to remove auto manufacturing from Canada entirely, Greer said the aim is to "re-industrialize" in general.

"I understand why the Canadians, you know, want to have as much as they can get and try to expand concessions from the U.S.," he said. "But we are focused on doing what's good for America and accommodating Canada to the extent we can."

Greer was the American lead on trade talks that fell apart last week. Both American and Canadian officials have said that U.S. tariffs on finished vehicles and Canadian auto parts were outstanding issues in those negotiations.

items: LeBlanc welcomes U.S. decision 'withdrawing positions' on language, culture
Trump's top trade negotiator disputes Canadian assertion that U.S. made last-minute demands

blocks.text: Canadian negotiators sought to have those tariffs reduced from the 25 per cent rate, but argued that the U.S. at the last minute sought to exclude heavy- and medium-sized trucks from that relief. The Americans, including Greer, dispute that the exclusion was a last-minute ask on their part.
Heavy and medium trucks would include some models of Ford's F-Series pickups and General Motors' Silverado which are both made at Ontario plants that employ roughly 20,000 workers.
Greer said medium- and heavy-duty truck duties were "separate" from the auto tariffs the Trump administration had offered lower.
WATCH | Canada 'will continue to fight' for auto jobs, says industry minister:
Canada 'will continue to fight' for auto jobs, says industry minister
Flavio Volpe, president of the Automotive Parts Manufactures' Association, said Greer's recent comments shouldn't come as a surprise.
"The president has said it, the secretary of commerce has said it … they want cars made in the U.S. and not in Canada and so you don't have to tell me that again," Volpe told CBC News.

Since the first few weeks of his second term, Trump has said "we don't need [Canada] to make our cars." The president repeated that claim in the Oval Office on Thursday after signing an executive order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America.
WATCH | Trump signs order to rename Lake Ontario:
Trump signs executive order to rename Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’

"We want to make the cars here. They can make their own cars if they want and they can continue to make their cars for Canada. But we don't want them to make cars for the United States of America," he said.

Last fall, Lutnick told an audience in Toronto that he wanted to use tariffs to drain auto assembly from Canada. Sources told CBC News just prior to last week's deal falling apart that Lutnick was dissatisfied with what was on the table, specifically around auto tariffs.
Auto rep 'encouraged' by Greer's remarks

Brian Kingston, president of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers' Association, said he's "encouraged" by Greer's comments on the goal of re-industrializing in the U.S. He said that industrializing the American automotive industry will by necessity include Canada.
"It's not unexpected that we're going to see heightened rhetoric following the breakdown of negotiations," Kingston told CBC News.

"[Greer] did not say 'Canada can't have an auto industry.' And in fact, Canada should be doing everything in its power to protect our industrial base and strengthen it. So how do we do that? We're going to do that by strengthening our auto industries together, which are tightly integrated."
Trump threatened to double tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles and non-CUSMA-compliant auto parts in the new year after the talks fell apart last week.
Kingston said continued retaliation will threaten the entirety of the North American auto industry.

"If we can't find an off ramp in lower tariff rates, it makes the industry across North America less competitive and therefore it will reduce their ability to compete with manufacturers in other parts of the world," he said.
WATCH | A closer look at Greer's comments:
How true are Jamieson Greer's claims on the Canada-U.S. trade fallout? | Hanomansing Tonight
Despite the breakdown in negotiations, Kingston said he thinks a deal is still within reach.
"Cooler heads will prevail. But we do need to stop the cycle of retaliation and start talking again," he said.
Volpe said he hopes the Trump administration realizes it doesn't make sense to separate the Canadian and American auto sectors.
"Countries don't make cars. Industries in those countries make cars," he said.
"When you have the ambassador come on and say Canada is the source of the decline of U.S. auto, that's like saying your right foot is the source of the pain in your left foot."

What we know about how the Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart

blocks.text: Volpe says he's encouraged by Greer conducting an interview with Canadian media, saying it could be a sign that the topic of Canada-U.S. trade is breaking through in the Trump administration.
He said regardless of where trade discussions go from here, Canada will have to own up to whatever deal it signs.

"If we do a deal that signs off the auto sector, then we own that. It's not the fault of the Trump administration who says that they want something from us. If we hand it to them, then it's on us," he said.

Shortly after 11:30 p.m. ET on March 22, an air traffic controller cleared an Air Canada Express plane to land less than two minutes before green-lighting a fire truck to cross the active runway. The resulting collision left two Canadian aviators dead and sent more than 40 people to hospital.

Conservationists have long been working to keep a rare species of bird from disappearing entirely from the United Kingdom.

But any recent success they've had in protecting the Montagu's harrier's British population can largely be attributed to the mating prowess of one "absolutely prolific" male, says conservationist Mark Thomas.
The 10-year-old stud in question is called AU — the chemical symbol for gold — and he's sired 16 juveniles over the course of his life, including 10 in the last two years.
"He's at the top of his game," Thomas, the species lead for Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB), told As It Happens guest host Paul Hunter.
"He is single-handedly propping up this species in the U.K. There's no two ways about it."
'It's been a great year'
Montagu's harriers are migratory birds of prey who spend their winters in Africa and parts of Asia, and return to Europe every spring to breed.
Globally, their population is on the decline, and listed as a species of least concern on the International Union for Conservation of Nature's Red List.
In the U.K., the RSPB says, the already rare birds have been rapidly declining, and threatening to disappear from the country altogether.

At their peak in the 1950s, there were about 30 breeding pairs in the U.K., which dropped to zero in the '70s, before rising back to 13 in the mid-aughts. That was followed by another steep decline when there were zero breeding pairs reported between 2000 and 2003.
"We're desperate to try and save the birds we have currently," Thomas said. "And it's been a great year."

blocks.caption: One of the two Montagu harrier nests in the U.K. this summer. (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds)

blocks.text: That's thanks to AU.
After successfully raising four chicks in 2025, the so-called "golden boy" returned again this year to do his acrobatic mating displays in the hopes of catching the eye of some willing females.
"He'll fly to, like, a thousand feet in the air and then he'll do these amazing twist and turns flashing his wings," Thomas said. "The females will then appear. They will chase him around."
This year, Thomas said, three females were fighting for AU's attention.
"The three had a big fight, and they got down to two. And then the two stayed, and nested with him."
Protecting the nests
AU fathered six chicks between his two mates, four female and two male.

Conservationists are hopeful that his sons will one day return to the U.K. to breed. Two of his male offspring from 2025 have already been spotted in the country, though they're not yet old enough to breed.
"That's really good new in terms of the population continuing," Thomas said.
The six new hatchlings are spread evenly among two nests, roughly one kilometre apart in a top-secret location, somewhere on a British farm.
Only the scientists and the landowners know where the nests are located, and the researchers constructed barriers around them to protect the baby birds from predators and other threats.
"This is one of the most exciting birds we have in the U.K. and to work on it is a dream every single day," Thomas said.
"It's also quite a lot of responsibility as well, you know, to know that you are handling the chicks of a bird that has only got two nests in the whole United Kingdom."

blocks.caption: A female Montagu's harrier chick is one of six of its species to hatch in the U.K. this year. (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds)

blocks.text: Montagu's harriers are a lowland species that prefer to nest in marshes and river plains. When no suitable habitat is available, they tend to nest instead among the crops on farmland, putting them at risk of being destroyed by agricultural machinery.
"So the RSPB's role is to find these nests, liaise with the farmers, work very closely with them and then safeguard the chicks in their nest," Thomas said.
Tracking the youngsters
That should be easier in the future, if all goes according to plan.
For the first time, the RSPB has attached satellite trackers to two juvenile harriers, one from each nest.

blocks.caption: For the first time, the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds has affixed two juvenile Montagu's harriers with satellite trackers. (Royal Society for the Protection of Birds)

blocks.text: The young birds will soon be ready to leave their nest and migrate, and the RSPB will be able to see exactly where they go, and where they end up should they return.
If they survive and return to the U.K. to breed, Thomas and his team should easily be able to find their nests and spring into action once again.
"We've never done this with juveniles before," he said. "So we're absolutely kind of, you know, on tenterhooks waiting to see what the data shows."
Interview with Mark Thomas produced by Sarah Jackson

articles.title: Jury deliberating in trial of Lindsay Clancy, US woman accused of killing her children
articles.summary: Prosecutors argued Clancy made a calculated decision to murder the children, while the defence argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details and discussion of attempted suicide

The fate of US mother Lindsay Clancy is now in the hands of a Massachusetts jury, who must decide if she is guilty of first-degree murder - the intentional and premeditated killing of another person - in the deaths of her three children.

For five weeks, the trial has gripped the country as Clancy's lawyers have argued that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis when she killed her children, who ranged in age from eight months to five years. Clancy does not deny killing her two sons and daughter.
The prosecution argued she made a calculated decision to intentionally murder them.
The jury could find Clancy guilty of first-degree murder, guilty of lesser charges, or not guilty.
The jury of nine women and three men completed their first day of deliberations on Thursday. They will return on Friday.
In the state of Massachusetts, a first-degree murder conviction carries a mandatory life in prison sentence without the possibility of parole.

The jury could instead find Clancy guilty of second-degree murder - committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning - or involuntary manslaughter - causing death because of extreme carelessness. Those convictions, too, would lead to some prison time.
If Clancy is found not guilty by reason of insanity, then she will not be set free, but instead sent to a psychiatric hospital, where she possibly could remain for life.
Attorneys for both sides made closing arguments on Thursday before the jury began deliberating.

Kevin Reddington, Clancy's lawyer, repeated the defence's argument that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she killed the children with exercise bands at their home and then attempted to end her own life by jumping out of a window. Clancy was paralysed by the attempt and has attended the trial in a wheelchair.

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect," Reddington said, adding that he believed prosecutors were "not going to be able to prove otherwise".

The UK's National Health Service (NHS) defines postpartum psychosis as a rare and serious mental health illness that can affect someone soon after having a baby, and which should be treated as a medical emergency.

One of the more tense moments of the closing arguments came when Reddington directly addressed the prosecutors and asked them to explain why they tried to prove Clancy's suicide attempt was not serious. The judge interrupted and ordered him to address only the jury.
Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague did not dispute that Clancy was mentally ill, but told the jury that the defendant could tell the difference between right and wrong at the time of the killings.

"It's not the system or the DSM that caused her to strangle her kids," Sprague told the jury, referencing the US encyclopaedia of mental heath diagnoses, which does not give postpartum psychosis its own classification.
Sprague also said Clancy had an "abundance of care", but had hidden thoughts from doctors about harming her kids.

If you are suffering distress or despair and need support, you could speak to a health professional, or an organisation that offers support. Details of help available in many countries can be found at Befrienders Worldwide. www.befrienders.org.
In the UK a list of organisations that can help is available at bbc.co.uk/actionline.

Leslie Crespi, a U.S.-based community liaison for the Isha Foundation in North America, a non-profit spirituality group, told CBC News Network on Thursday that the 10 are among 80 members of the foundation still missing.
The 10 were among 12 Canadians on the trek, Crespi said.

The co-ordinator of the trek contacted the Isha Foundation at 9:07 a.m. on Wednesday, after the group arrived at an Chinese immigration centre in Gyirong County, Tibet. The flash flooding hit that particular area at 9:14 a.m., she said.

blocks.text: Parents and teachers at the epicentre of the Democratic Republic of Congo's fast-moving Ebola outbreak are urging authorities to delay the reopening of schools as infections continue to outpace efforts to contain the disease.

The Ebola outbreak, centred in the eastern Ituri province, is the fastest-growing in the disease's history and remains out of control with 5,713 confirmed cases, including 2,744 deaths, according to Congolese health authorities.

On Thursday, officials with Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention said weekly cases and deaths are still rising in Ituri and the neighbouring province of Nord Kivu — and warned that the scale of the outbreak may be far larger than tallies have indicated.

Kyeng Mercy, a public health strategist and epidemiologist with Africa CDC, estimated that only 30 to 40 per cent of cases are being detected. Counts of cases coming from known contacts and other indicators suggested "underdetection" in communities, she added.
"So with all this, we're seeing that this outbreak could be three times larger than the current actual size that is being recorded," she said.
'Not at the cost of our lives'
Children aged four and below have the highest case-fatality rate of any age group in the outbreak, at 60 per cent, according to the World Health Organization Regional Office for Africa.

Schools are set to reopen across Congo on Sept. 1, but some teachers and parents in Ituri are urging authorities to delay the return, saying the Ebola outbreak still poses too great a risk to children.

"We want to resume classes, but not at the cost of our lives," Fazila Rebecca, a teacher in Ituri's capital of Bunia, told The Associated Press. "As long as the disease is circulating and protective measures remain inadequate, returning to the classroom means taking a risk we cannot ignore."
WATCH | Experts say it will be months before the outbreak is under control:
It’ll take at least 6 months to contain Ebola outbreak in Congo: experts

The local Ituri teachers union met Tuesday in Bunia, urging authorities to assess the outbreak before deciding whether to reopen schools. Authorities in Ituri did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Yap Boum, who leads emergency preparedness and response at Africa CDC, said officials have sped up training for teachers so they are well informed about the disease. They will check students’ temperatures upon arrival, Boum said, and because clean water is not always readily available, sanitizing alcoholic gel is being provided.

United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Thursday that an additional $1.1 billion US is urgently needed to fight the outbreak, with the United Nation's $2.13 billion response plan only 48 per cent funded — largely because of a major contribution from the United States.

Guterres said international attention and resources are still lagging behind the reality on the ground, warning that "without additional funding, vital operations will run out of money just when they need to expand."
WATCH | The outbreak has now become the country's deadliest:
Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history

The outbreak in eastern D.R.C. is spreading under extremely difficult conditions, fuelled by insecurity, displacement, a health workers' strike and intense population movements. The World Health Organization has said it remains out of control and is on track to surpass the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, the deadliest on record, which killed more than 11,000 people.

Although the current outbreak was declared in mid-May, officials believe it had been spreading since February. It has spread from three health zones to nearly 60, with most cases and deaths occurring outside the network of monitored contacts and within communities.
No approved treatments

A key challenge in fighting the outbreak is that the rare Bundibugyo virus that is causing it has no approved vaccines or treatments, although clinical trials of potential vaccines and treatments have begun in D.R.C. as well as Canada and the U.K.

Two studies are also under way to examine the effectiveness of the Ervebo vaccine, which was developed to treat the Zaire Ebola strain and which earlier studies have shown may provide cross protection against the Bundibugyo strain. In one of those trials, frontline workers have now started receiving doses of the Ervebo vaccine, said Placide Mbala Kingebeni, who oversees Africa CDC's research, clinical trials and innovation efforts.

Efforts to bring the outbreak under control — from limited public gatherings to social distancing and airport closures — have disrupted life in the six affected provinces, particularly Ituri, which has been ravaged by rebel violence.

blocks.text: The government has introduced measures, including installing health and sanitary equipment at some locations, but advocacy groups say more needs to be done to build trust within the community.
"Beyond the practical challenges, community acceptance remains critical," said Greg Ramm, director for Save the Children in D.R.C.
"The immediate priority is to ensure that every school, teacher and family has the information and resources they need to make the start of the school year as safe as possible for children."
Espérance Dz'venga was shopping for school supplies Wednesday at Bunia's central market. She said she wants her children in school, but worries about their safety.

"As a parent, I want to see my children in school, but — like many other parents — what I want most is for them to come home healthy," she said. "We are afraid that our children might be exposed at school and then bring the illness home."

blocks.text: Artist Yayoi Kusama transfixed the world with her unique perspective — often expressed by blanketing her canvases, sculptures and museum installations in a mesmerizing, endless swarm of her trademark polka dots.

Kusama, whose death at 97 in a hospital in Tokyo was announced on Thursday by her studio, became one of Japan's most revered contemporary artists. Her art travelled the globe to be exhibited in famous galleries, including the Museum of Modern Art and the Whitney Museum of American Art in New York, and the Museum Ludwig in Germany.

blocks.caption: People walk through the art installation Infinity Mirror Room during a preview of the new major exhibition of legendary Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany, in March. (Martin Meissner/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Perhaps among her most famous creations, her Infinity Mirror Rooms installations have spawned long queues at museums, including at Toronto's Art Gallery of Ontario where visitors flocked to see the Yayoi Kusama: Infinity Mirrors exhibition in 2018. The show's popularity led the gallery to purchase, with crowdfunded support, the permanent installation Infinity Mirrored Room — Let's Survive Forever.

blocks.caption: Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli's Field features Kusama's signature polka dots on stuffed phallic shapes surrounded by mirrors. Standing in the room alone, as the piece is meant to be experienced, creates a hallucinatory scene with the viewer's reflection making them an unavoidable part of the expe…

The pumpkin motif appears in many of Kusama's works dating to the 1940s and, in 1993, this piece, titled All the Eternal Love I Have for the Pumpkin, appeared in the Venice Biennale. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Like her signature orange bob wig, her works have become instantly recognizable, featuring her trademark repetitive psychedelic motifs that include bright, colourful swirls, worms, netting, and most often polka dots, sparkling balls or dots of lights.

blocks.caption: Kusama is seen wearing Louis Vuitton, a fashion brand she partnered with in 2012. (Steve Eichner/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images)
Kusama visited Paris for her multi-site exhibition on in 2001. (Alain Nogues/Sygma/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Kusama frequently said she painted the way she saw the world: covered in spots, much like the hallucinations she said she had from childhood.

blocks.caption: A woman views the artwork My Eternal Soul Series during a preview of an exhibition of Kusama's work at the Museum Ludwig in March. (Martin Meissner/The Associated Press)
The sculpture A Bouquet of Love I Saw In the Universe by Kusama is seen at an exhibition at Martin-Gropius-Bau in April 2021 in Berlin. (Adam Berry/Getty Images)

Visitors stand inside Kusama's metal, fibreglass, urethane, paint and stickers installation titled With All My Love for the Tulips, I Pray Forever, 2013 at National Gallery Singapore in June 2017 in Singapore. (Suhaimi Abdullah/Getty Images)

blocks.text: She dealt with years of mental health challenges and recurring visits to psychiatric institutions and was once ostracized by the cultural elite in Japan for her avant-garde style, according to the New York Times. And yet despite those challenges, the artist, whose canon includes installations with phallic fabric sculptures and naked performance pieces, provoked public discourse and became a fixture of the art world.

blocks.caption: An art installation of furniture, clothing and other items covered in phallic-like objects is seen in New York in 2012. (Steve Eichner/WWD/Penske Media/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Kusama was born in 1929 in Matsumoto, Japan, and moved to the United States to pursue her art in 1957.

In the late '60s, while Kusama lived in New York City, she held "happening" antiwar performances where she painted circles on people's bodies and, once, even a horse. While the performances gained media attention they also resulted in arrests for obscenity.

blocks.caption: At Kusama's 'happening' antiwar performances, like this one on July 14, 1967, she painted circles on people's bodies. (Seymour Wally/NY Daily News/Getty Images)
Kusama's I Spend Each Day Embracing Flowers is seen at David Zwirner's 19th street gallery in New York City in 2023. (Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

blocks.text: "I want to create a thousand paintings, maybe two thousand paintings, as many as I can draw," she told The Associated Press during an interview in 2012. "I will keep painting until I die."

blocks.caption: Paintings and flower sculptures with the title Flowers that Bloom Now appear at the David Zwirner gallery in New York City in 2017. (Stephanie Ott/picture alliance/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As her fame grew, fashion brands began to take notice. Kusama signed on with Louis Vuitton in 2012 under then-creative director Marc Jacobs. She also signed on with other licensed products, with her illustrations appearing on teacups, key chains and T-shirts.

blocks.caption: Yayoi Kusama x Louis Vuitton immersive fashion and art pop-up is seen at Harrods in 2023 in London. (Jim Dyson/Getty Images)

A sculpture of Yayoi Kusama sits atop the Louis Vuitton's Champs Elysees store in 2023 in Paris. Kusama licensed her art for many products, including teacups, key chains and T-shirts. (Edward Berthelot/Getty Images)
Kusama, centre, appears with Louis Vuitton leadership at the Louis Vuitton and Yayoi Kusama collaboration unveiling event in New York City in 2012. (Neilson Barnard/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Kusama was a visionary not only on canvas and sculpture but in other mediums; the artist was also a filmmaker and author, having published several novels. She told The Associated Press that her creative process was so mysterious that there were times when she even surprised herself.
"I think, 'Oh I drew that? I was thinking that,'" she said.

blocks.caption: Dots Obsession: Infinity Mirrored Room is seen in 2008 at the contemporary art centre Le Spot in Le Havre, France. (Robert Francois/AFP/Getty Images)
A tourist looks at Kusama's Yellow Pumpkin sculpture in Naoshima, Japan. (Education Images/Universal Images Group/Getty Images)
Kusama's Love Forever features hexagonal mirrors surrounding two peepholes through which viewers can see their faces repeated infinitely. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

articles.title: Judge rejects application by 'Surrey Six' killer to stay convictions
articles.summary: A B.C. Supreme Court judge has rejected an application by one of the "Surrey Six" killers to stay the convictions against him.

image.caption: Cody Haevischer watched from the prisoner's box as B.C. Supreme Court Justice Martha Devlin rejected his application for a stay of proceedings in the Surrey Six case. Haevischer will have to serve a life sentence for six counts of murder and one count of conspiracy to commit murder. (Sheila Allan/CB

blocks.text: A B.C. Supreme Court judge has rejected an application by one of the Surrey Six killers to stay the convictions against him.

Nearly 20 years after a gangland slaying that shocked the province, Justice Martha Devlin said Thursday that allegations of abuse of process levelled by Cody Haevischer against police and corrections officials did not rise to the level that would have seen her stay the case against him.

The judge's decision resulted in six convictions for murder and one count of conspiracy to commit murder against Haevischer being officially entered into the judicial record — meaning the gangster must serve a life sentence for his crimes.
A lengthy legal battle

Haevischer — who was found guilty in the Surrey Six murders in 2014 — sought a stay of proceedings before the convictions could be entered, claiming police misconduct and his treatment behind bars amounted to an abuse of process.

He was asking for a stay of proceedings or a reduction in his sentence to 25 years, but after a lengthy consideration of all Haevischer's allegations, Devlin rejected all but a handful of his claims, finding only that time in solitary confinement had breached the killer's Charter rights.

blocks.caption: Eileen Mohan's son, Christopher, was one of two innocent Surrey Six victims. She applauded a decision to dismiss an application to stay proceedings brought by one of the killers. (Jason Proctor/CBC)

blocks.text: "I have concluded that the vast majority of Mr. Haevischer's allegations simply have no merit," Devlin said at the conclusion of a lengthy reading of a 60-page summary of her findings.
"The remaining aspects of his applications which do rise to the level of an abuse of process do not satisfy the 'clearest of cases,' which must be met for a stay of proceedings."
Devlin's ruling follows a long and complicated legal history arising from the murders in October 2007.

Haevischer and co-accused Matthew Johnston were arrested and charged in the crimes in 2009. Prior to that, a third killer — known as Person X — pleaded guilty to three counts of second-degree murder and one count of conspiracy in relation to the killings.
In December 2014, Haevischer and Johnston were found guilty, but they applied for a stay of proceedings before their convictions were entered into the record.

The judge who initially found them guilty summarily dismissed the application — meaning she didn't hold an evidentiary hearing — because the charges against them were so serious the killers weren't going to be let go as a remedy for abuse of process.

But B.C.'s Court of Appeal overturned that decision, quashing the convictions. The appeal court ruling was upheld by the Supreme Court of Canada and the matter was set for an evidentiary hearing, which began in November 2024.
Johnston died in pretrial custody during the course of the proceedings.
'One notorious incident stands alone'
Devlin's ruling drew gasps from the public gallery, which was filled with victims' family members, who later embraced outside the courtroom.
Eileen Mohan, whose son Christopher was one of two innocent victims, called the decision a "glorious verdict."

blocks.caption: Christopher Mohan, 22, was one of two innocent victims shot dead in the Surrey Six killings. (Facebook)

blocks.text: "It gives us satisfaction that at least there's justice for our loved ones, and the courts have spoken today," Mohan said on the courthouse steps.

"I applaud her for not just giving me hope, but giving the people of British Columbia hope that you can't just walk to the doorstep of my home, steal my innocent son's life and expect to walk free from the courts."
In her opening remarks, Devlin noted that nearly 20 years have passed since the Surrey Six murders shocked the province during what she called gang "warfare of an unprecedented scale."
But even amid that violence, Devlin said "one notorious incident stands alone."

items: More stories from Vancouver-South Coast

blocks.text: The Surrey Six murders occurred on Oct. 19, 2007, when Haevischer and other Red Scorpion gang members went to the apartment of drug dealer Corey Lal to kill him for failing to pay a "tax."

But along with Lal, the killers encountered five other people, including two innocent victims: a 22-year-old who lived on the same floor and a repair man servicing fireplaces in the apartment building.
Devlin said the killers separated the six victims into two groups of three and shot them in the back and head.
Some of them had their heads covered, and police testified that they were in submissive positions.
No matter what proceedings have occurred in the years since, and despite his attempts to minimize his involvement, Devlin said the facts of the findings against Haevischer remain unchallenged.
"In a calculated and deliberate matter, he decided to murder all six victims and actively participated in their execution," she said.
"Mr. Haevischer extinguished the lives of six defenceless men."
'The clearest of cases'

The fundamental questions Devlin was facing were whether Haevischer's allegations of police impropriety and his treatment in custody constituted an abuse of process that would undermine his right to a fair trial or bring the justice system into disrepute.

And even if an abuse of process existed, Devlin said she also had to consider whether it would be the "clearest of cases," which deserved a remedy such as a stay of proceedings or a reduction in Haevischer's sentence from life in prison to 25 years.

The allegations of abuse of process fell into two broad categories: police misconduct involving allegations that officers manipulated and engaged in sexual conduct with vulnerable witnesses; and claims related to Haevischer's time in custody prior to and during his trial.

Devlin methodically assessed each incident of alleged police abuse, including sexual relationships between senior RCMP officers and female witnesses that resulted in disciplinary proceedings and criminal charges against the officers.

But in those cases, Devlin said there was no evidence that the events occurred with the approval of the RCMP. If anything, she said, the officers involved were aware that their actions could imperil the case.

She also said Haevischer's allegations of witness manipulation failed to take into account the bravery of female witnesses — including former girlfriends of gang members — who gave evidence in spite of great personal risk.

Devlin accepted the fact that Haevischer's time in segregation in the year after his arrest, combined with limits on his interactions with other human beings, amounted to a level of solitary confinement that breached his Charter right to life, liberty and security of the person.
But she rejected the notion that B.C. Corrections officials had acted at the behest of police in order to put pressure on Haevischer.
Devlin said it was understandable that pretrial staff would worry about the impact of the arrival of a high-profile gang member into a prison population filled with members of rival gangs.

She said there were also legitimate concerns about Haevischer's potential to manipulate other inmates, and that while his treatment would not be acceptable by today's standards, it was accepted at the time.

The judge also questioned Haevischer's claims that the anxiety he suffers today is solely due to his treatment behind bars, noting that he failed to account for the effects of threats to his life through gang conflict, the prospect of a high-stakes trial and a child custody battle.

At the conclusion of her ruling, Devlin entered the convictions against Haevischer into the record. He also faces sentencing for a contempt of court conviction for refusing to give evidence during the proceedings, citing a supposed "inmate code."

blocks.text: Three of Canada's big banks shared cautiously sunny outlooks for the economy on Thursday, sharply contrasting expressions of anxiety and frustration from scores of smaller businesses grappling with the fresh reality of a full-blown trade war with the United States.
Royal Bank of Canada, Toronto-Dominion Bank and CIBC reported financial results before Thursday's opening bell on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

Together, this trio of Canadian banking giants has as much as $6 trillion worth of assets on their balance sheets. With vast portfolios of mortgages, auto loans and other debt products for consumers and businesses, and client networks spanning Canada and the U.S., these goliath institutions have a unique vantage point from which to monitor the impact of tariffs.

"The Canadian economy has proven to be resilient. The improvements in employment and GDP seen in Q2 maintain a cautiously optimistic outlook that the economy will continue to expand," RBC CEO Dave McKay said on the bank's quarterly conference call Thursday morning.

"While Canada and the U.S. have yet to come to a longer-term solution, we note the average effective tariff rate remains low, at approximately six percent, with over 80 per cent of exports remaining duty-free.”
Investment 'super cycle' to the rescue

On Thursday, TD Bank CEO Raymond Chun referred to an emerging "super cycle" for investment in Canada, spurred by government spending in areas like infrastructure and national defence. According to TD Economics, Ottawa and the provinces have over $1 trillion in announced projects already approved or on the table through 2035 and beyond.
"In Canada, trade tensions have not dampened investment opportunities, as governments seek to drive new activity," Chun said.
"More could be rolled out across Canada over the coming decade in a historic investment super cycle," he added. "We are very well positioned to benefit from this activity."
CIBC CEO Harry Culham said he has "measured confidence" about the back half of 2026.
"The trade environment will continue to evolve, and we are not going to speculate on where it lands," he said on Thursday, speaking on his bank's conference call with stock market analysts.
CIBC chief risk officer Frank Guse said that CIBC is closely monitoring Canada's labour market for signs of weakness.
A recent Oxford Economics study prepared for the Canadian American Business Council found more than 100,000 Canadian jobs could be lost if the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) was eliminated.
BMO Capital Markets predicts the latest round of U.S. tariffs will carve roughly half a percentage point from Canadian growth, mostly through weaker business confidence and investment.

On Wednesday, National Bank's CEO Laurent Ferreira said Canada's economy has "demonstrated resilience" over the past 18 months. Like his peers, he also praised Ottawa's large-scale investment plans, as well as the newly announced government aid measures for workers and businesses impacted by U.S. tariffs.

"Energy, power infrastructure, and the recent icebreaker contract announcement are great examples of our country moving in the right direction," Ferreira said, referring to a commitment announced by the federal government to build six icebreaker ships in Quebec.
He also praised the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions' June decision to lower its domestic stability buffer, allowing banks more flexability to lend to struggling businesses.
On Tuesday, the CEO of Bank of Montreal and Scotiabank separately called the Canada-U.S. trade war manageable.

On the Toronto Stock Exchange, shares of Canada's big banks continue to trade near all-time highs. The iShares S&P/TSX Capped Energy Index ETF, a basket of Canadian bank stocks, has soared over 46 per cent year-to-date.

articles.title: Allan Little: I met dangerously fanatical Mladić early in Bosnian war
articles.summary: BBC special correspondent Allan Little met the "Butcher of Bosnia" in the early months of the Bosnian war.

blocks.text: Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić, dubbed the "Butcher of Bosnia" for his actions during the Balkan wars of the 1990s, has died in prison.
BBC special correspondent Allan Little was there throughout the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, and met Mladić in the early months of the Bosnian war.
At night, you could watch the fires of ethnic cleansing across the landscape. The flames provided the only light under the night sky and the black valley would glimmer with flecks of orange.

You could watch the men of our village move about silently in the shadows of their homes, each armed with some ancient weapon salvaged from wars long ago and, like the fears and the suspicions and the distrusts, handed down through the generations.
One morning I watched a procession of men and women emerge from a forest. They had been driven from their homes two days earlier and had fled with what they could carry.

Most were on foot. Some were crammed into the back of ancient farm vehicles drawn by donkeys. There were perhaps 40,000 of them. Their home town had fallen to a Serb advance that had come without warning.
Among them, one man seemed close to collapse. He stopped to speak to us.

The whole town had fled, he said. He had become separated from his wife in the long trek to safety and was now worried that she had not made it. His pale, almost translucently white skin was stretched across the bones of his face like parchment. His forehead was livid blue from a fall.
I asked him how old he was. He said he was 80. "May I ask" I said, "are you a Croat or a Muslim?"
The memory of it shames me even now as I hear, in my mind, his answer echo down the years.
"I am," he said, "a musician".

Our convenient ethnic shorthand reduced them to Serbs, Croats and Muslims. But they were also musicians and scientists and doctors and plumbers and farmers and mothers and fathers and brothers and sisters and very often children.

I met Mladić in that first hot summer of the war in Bosnia. We were at Lukavica barracks on the southern edge of Sarajevo. The barracks was awash with weapons and the menacing strut of the paramilitaries.
You could buy a Kalashnikov for 200 dollars, a hand grenade for just one dollar – the same price, I would soon learn, as the cost of a fresh egg in the besieged city.

I shook his hand and he held it fast and pulled me in close. He told me he had just come back from the Sarajevo city centre front line and I saw that he was pumped up by the exhilarating proximity of the fighting.

He held my hand for many minutes, fixed me with his eye and told me he was the great defender of brotherhood and unity in former Yugoslavia, and that he dreamed of a world in which there would no guns and no war. He struck me then as fanatical, dangerously so.

In the years that lay ahead, forces under his command committed the worst war crimes on European soil since the Nazis. They bequeathed to the lexicon of war a grim new euphemism - ethnic cleansing. They committed mass murder, extermination, mass rape, forced expulsions. They burned village after village, all in the name of creating an ethnically pure Serbian territory in Croatia and Serbia. Ultimately, at Srebrenica, they committed genocide.
Two days after I had met the old musician on that damp muddy roadside, I found myself drawn into the passions of the war in a personal and – at the time – devastating way.

My cameraman, Tihomir Tunukovic, a man I had known and worked alongside during the previous 18 months, was killed by a Serb gunner on a ridge above the road he was driving on. We had parted earlier that morning. He was 25 years old, a talented and ambitious young film maker from Zagreb.

We drove his body back along the rutted mountain pathways to the coastal city of Split. We broke our hearts at his funeral. The grief of it connected us to the sentiments of the war – the impulse to vengeance and counter vengeance – that were so much a feature of what we were witnessing.
General Mladić did not pull the trigger but his command created an atmosphere of wanton permissiveness which cost tens of thousands of lives.

articles.title: Norwegians lay flowers at palace as King Harald's condition worsens
articles.summary: The 89-year-old's condition is described as "extremely serious" and members of his family have visited him in hospital.

blocks.text: Having been on the throne since 1991, King Harald is Europe's oldest head of state.
Crown Prince Haakon, 53, the successor to the Norwegian throne, has been serving as regent while his father is on leave.

King Harald has been treated in recent weeks with cortisone for haemolytic anaemia, a condition that causes the number of red blood cells in the body to be reduced, and leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.

There was a sombre mood in Oslo as Norwegians followed the comings and goings of the royal family. Crowds milled around in Palace Square throughout the day as Norwegian public TV scrapped its schedule to cover the story.
Although no-one in the royal family spoke, the message was clear that it had become an important moment to visit the king.

Among those visiting the hospital were Crown Princess Mette-Marit who arrived with Haakon, as well as her son Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest during his appeal against a conviction for rape.
King Harald's sister, Princess Astrid, also visited the hospital, along with Haakon and Mette-Marit's children Princess Ingrid Alexandra and Prince Sverre Magnus.
Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre cancelled a planned trip to Germany, where he was expected to meet Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Thursday.
"The whole nation is with us as we send warm thoughts to the king and the rest of the royal family," he said in a statement.

articles.title: Two killed in 'domestic violence incident' at school near Berlin
articles.summary: Police have arrested a 19-year-old male suspect after an incident in which two people were killed near the German capital.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed in a "domestic violence incident" at a school in the town of Gosen-Neu Zittau near the German capital Berlin, local police have said.
Brandenburg state police said they arrested a 19-year-old German man, who is "considered a prime suspect". They said it was not a "mass shooting", without specifying what weapon was used.
It is not yet known if the suspect was a student at the private Docemus school.
One of the dead was an 18-year-old secondary school female student and the other victim was a 30-year-old man who died when he tried to intervene, local media reported.
The arrested suspect is believed to be the ex-boyfriend of the 18-year-old victim, Maz Online reported.
Ulrike Liedtke, the speaker of Brandenburg's regional parliament, called the incident a "cowardly femicide".
"The fact that we once again had to witness deadly violence against a woman fills me with deep sorrow and anger.
"I am shaken that a citizen who showed moral courage and wanted to help also lost his life in this terrible act," Liedtke said.
State premier Dietmar Woidke said it was an "unimaginable act of violence".
The school's managing director Michael Kunz said classes will be cancelled on Friday.
Although there would be no regular classes, Kunz said the school would remain open for all students who wished to come.
"We want to provide them with a safe space where they can come together, talk to each other, and process what has happened," he said.
A "very careful" decision will be made in coming days about how school life will be structured, he added.
Last month in a separate attack, two girls were seriously wounded and a 16-year-old suspect arrested at a secondary school in southern Germany.

articles.title: Convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Mladić dies aged 84
articles.summary: He was jailed for life in 2017 for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity during the wars in the ex-Yugoslavia in 1992-95.

blocks.text: Mladić - who never recognised the UN court - had been held at The Hague detention facility since 2011.
He commanded Bosnian Serb forces in the 1990s against the Bosnian Croat and Bosniak (Bosnian Muslim) armies.

During the war his troops committed what became known as "ethnic cleansing" in Bosnia-Herzegovina in a bid to expel the non-Serbian population by force. They besieged the main city of Sarajevo with the deaths of more than 10,000 people, and carried out the massacre of 8,000 men and boys at Srebrenica.

Hasan Hasanović , a Srebrenica survivor who lost his twin brother and father in the massacre, told the BBC World Service's Newshour programme that Mladić's death "does not bring closure because the people who were killed in Srebrenica cannot come back".

"His death is just a biological necessity, and it doesn't bring to an end the political project and military project that created that legacy of genocide. And we now live with the consequences of a divided country, genocide denial," said Hasanović, who now works at the Srebrenica memorial centre.
However, Bosnian Serb separatist leader Milorad Dodik told Reuters news agency that Mladić "was respected by Serbian people. As a commander he stood to defend Serbs."
In Serbia's capital Belgrade, some local residents also praised him.
"I genuinely believe he protected the Serbian people, because after all, that was his duty," a man called Milan was quoted as saying by Reuters.
Another man, Vasilije, said: "It's a massive shame, it really is. Personally, I think it's a total injustice that he was even thrown in The Hague."

articles.title: What we should make of CIA boss's secret trip to Moscow
articles.summary: There is nothing routine about John Ratcliffe making a secret, 10,000-mile return dash to Moscow, writes Frank Gardner.

blocks.text: One US official told Politico that the "meeting was primarily to warn Russia against any escalatory action against the Baltic states".

The UK is also in Russian crosshairs. On Thursday, a foreign ministry spokeswoman said Russia could strike British military targets as retaliation for Ukrainian strikes on Russia using British missiles.
And a drone carrying an explosive which was discovered at an airport in the German city of Leipzig was probably Russian, security experts have said.
News of Ratcliffe's visit follows reports of US intelligence assessments that President Vladimir Putin was planning a limited assault on a Nato ally.

But you don't need the world's most powerful electronic eavesdropping organisation – the US National Security Agency – to know that Putin is under mounting domestic pressure to "do something" to break the deadlock.
Ukraine's deep strikes with long-range drones have not only hammered Russia's energy industry, they have brought the war home to ordinary Russians.

Nothing says things are not going to plan more than long queues for petrol and billowing smoke coming from stricken oil refineries. The Kremlin sees these attacks as Nato fighting an indirect war on Russia by using Ukraine as a proxy.
So how will Russia respond? There is a broad spectrum of possibilities here.

These include stepping up the ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine that Moscow is already launching, including targeting the centre of Kyiv, knowing that Ukraine is running dangerously low on Patriot interceptors to stop them.

Putin will be well aware of Donald Trump's periodic disdain for Nato and he may have calculated that a low-key attack on say, Lithuania, is not going to trigger Nato's mutual self-defence clause – Article 5 – and that the US will not respond.
In which case it would make sense for part of the CIA chief's unexplained mission to Moscow was to remind Russia that the US is still fully committed to Article 5.

Lithuania is of special interest to the Kremlin as it has a common border with Poland known as the "Suwalki Gap". Just 60 miles long, this strip of land is all that separates Russia's client state Belarus from its nuclear-armed exclave of Kaliningrad, which is separated from mainland Russia.
If Russia were to seize that it would effectively cut off those three Baltic states by land from their Nato neighbours.

Then there is the question of tactical nuclear warheads. It has long been said that Russian military doctrine views these small but highly destructive weapons as an integral part of its order of battle.
Moscow has been warned off, by friend and foe alike, not to break the 81-year long taboo on using nuclear weapons in anger.

Yet this could still be a tempting option for Vladimir Putin to "escalate to de-escalate" by demonstrating to Ukraine that it has such catastrophic weapons at its disposal it would be better for Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow's terms now or face annihilation.
Of course, in the absence of any clear, attributable, official confirmation from the US as to what this sudden CIA dash to Moscow was all about then it is always possible it was about something else.
That could be trying to persuade Russia to end its military cooperation with Iran, for example, or maybe about more prisoner swaps or the prospect of a mass mobilisation of Russian troops.
But make no mistake, this trip was highly unusual and it came at a time of rising tension between Moscow and the West. Something is almost certainly up.

articles.summary: Ratko Mladic, convicted of genocide for orchestrating the 1995 Srebrenica massacre of at least 8,000 Muslims in Europe's worst atrocity since the Second World War, has died.

Was among trio convicted by UN court for massacring Muslims in former Yugoslavia
