blocks.text: Dolly Parton was more than a musician, actor, author, philanthropist, or theme-park entrepreneur. Parton, who died Tuesday at age 80, occupied a space in our global cultural imagination — a figure of American mythology, someone best described as larger-than-life and then a little bit more. But from the very beginning, at the heart of everything she accomplished, she was a songwriter.

Selecting 11 songs across her many decades of recorded music is a fool’s errand, but there are some classics that stand above others. Here are a few across her discography — from country songs that challenge traditional gender dynamics to the greatest ballad ever committed to record.
1968: “Just Because I’m a Woman”

Parton was long celebrated for the feminist themes throughout her music. That progressive sociopolitical stance is evident from the beginning of her career, which overlapped with the emergence of the women’s liberation movement. On the country classic “Just Because I’m a Woman,” Parton’s protagonist reminds her partner he need not judge her for having previous sexual partners — after all, he’s had some, too. “My mistakes are no worse than yours,” she sings, “Just because I’m a woman.” She said the song was inspired by a conversation with her late husband, Carl Dean, who asked her if she’d been with any men before they met.
1971: “Coat of Many Colors”

The quintessential example of Parton the raconteur is “Coat of Many Colors.” It’s an autobiographical tale about her mother, who made a coat for Parton out of rags. She was mocked by other kids but understood its value. “Now I know we had no money, but I was rich as I could be,” she sings, “In my coat of many colors my momma made for me.”
1973: “Jolene”

It is not only one of Parton’s best-known hits, but also one of the best-known country music songs of all time. “Jolene” was inspired by Dean; Parton told NPR in 2008 that she wrote the song about a flirty bank teller who seemed to take an interest in him.

“She got this terrible crush on my husband,” she said. “And he just loved going to the bank because she paid him so much attention. It was kinda like a running joke between us — when I was saying, ‘Hell, you’re spending a lot of time at the bank. I don’t believe we’ve got that kind of money.’ So, it’s really an innocent song all around, but sounds like a dreadful one.”
1974: “I Will Always Love You”

The second single from Parton’s 13th studio album, “I Will Always Love You” is most known for its rendition by Whitney Houston. But the Parton original was written for Porter Wagoner ahead of her departure from “The Porter Wagoner Show.” (She left in 1974, having collaborated with him since 1967.) There have been several versions, but none as resonant as Houston’s, recorded in 1992 for the soundtrack to “The Bodyguard.” The song topped the all-genre Billboard Hot 100, where it stayed for a then-record-breaking 14 weeks.
1977: “Here You Come Again”

Parton wrote an overwhelming number of her hits, which makes “Here You Come Again” an interesting outlier. It was penned by Barry Mann and Cynthia Weil, first recorded by B.J. Thomas and originally conceived with the idea that Brenda Lee would record it. The song made its way to Parton and became a tentpole pop crossover hit for the country artist. But make no mistake — Parton made sure the steel guitar was heard loud and proud.

Enter Parton, the Hollywood star. It begins with the sound of a typewriter. (That clacking sound? Parton originally conceived of it by striking her long acrylic nails together.) The ebullient “9 to 5” was written for the 1980 film of the same name, which starred Jane Fonda, Lily Tomlin and Parton in her acting debut. The song also appears on her album “9 to 5 and Odd Jobs.” Lyrically, it celebrates women in the workplace and serves as a battle cry for pay equity; it earned Parton her first Oscar nomination.
1983: “Islands in the Stream,” with Kenny Rogers

By the 1980s, Parton had fashioned herself as a mainstream celebrity. On “Islands in the Stream” with Kenny Rogers, her clarion soprano makes for perfect harmonies. That shouldn’t come as any surprise, but perhaps this will: The song was written by the Bee Gees. Barry Gibb maintained it was meant for Diana Ross, while Robin Gibb said it was meant for Marvin Gaye. Whatever the case, it got to Parton and Rogers, and the rest is history. It’s also a reminder of how R&B and country music are inextricably linked.

blocks.caption: Dolly Parton, left, and Kenny Rogers rehearse a song for their appearance on the TV show “Live… And in Person” in Los Angeles on Sept. 27, 1983. (AP Photo/Doug Pizac, File)

blocks.text: 1989: “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That”

Before this triumphant return to capital-C country music, there was a deeper detour into ’80s drum machine-heavy pop. (If there’s a single Parton album to consider skipping, it is 1987’s “Rainbow.”) But what came after, 1989’s “White Limozeen,” should be celebrated for “Why’d You Come in Here Lookin’ Like That,” with its steel guitar, banjo, mandolins, Pedabro and a fierce fiddle courtesy of Ricky Skaggs — all while Parton playfully objectifies a man with a cheeky wink.
1999: “The Grass Is Blue”

“I’ve had to think up a way to survive,” Parton opens the title track to her 1999 album “The Grass Is Blue.” She said she wrote the bluegrass ballad in 30 minutes, during a lunch break while filming “Blue Valley Songbird,” a made-for-television musical drama about a woman who tries to leave an abusive partner. It features her scratch vocals — a demo meant to serve as a blueprint for the final recording — providing an additional rawness to a song of impossible pain. “And the sky is green / and the grass is blue,” she sings. “And I don’t love you.”
2001: “Little Sparrow”

If there is anything resembling a dip in Parton’s overwhelming popularity, it arrived in the ’90s, when country listeners instead embraced the glossy pop-country of Shania Twain and LeAnn Rimes. A pivot arrived at the end of that decade and into the one that followed, when Parton endeavored to make roots albums — pulling from bluegrass, country, gospel and Appalachian folk — that reinvigorated her music career. The heartbreaking a cappella harmonies of the title track on her 2001 album “Little Sparrow,” released one year after the death of her father and dedicated to him, are further evidence of her greatness. Parton’s is a voice that knows no bounds. But to remind people of that fact? Sometimes it takes going back home.
2014: “Blue Smoke”

No one writes place like Parton. On “Blue Smoke,” with its youthful choo-choo spirit, Parton brings the listener into her childhood home in the Blue Ridge Mountains, gorgeous, desolate and nostalgic. “Blue Smoke climbin’ up the mountain, Blue Smoke windin’ ’round the bend / Blue Smoke is the name of the heartbreak train that I am ridin’ in,” she sings. “I left a note, I wrote, ‘I’m leaving and I won’t be coming back’ / Blue Smoke rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling, rolling down the track.”
Philanthropic works

Beyond her music and entertainment career, Parton has built a lasting philanthropic legacy, particularly in education and literacy. In 1988, she established the Dollywood Foundation, initially focusing on scholarships for students in her hometown of Sevier County, Tennessee.

Her best-known initiative, Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library, was launched in 1995 as a way to encourage children to develop a love for reading. Inspired in part by her father, who could not read or write, the program began by sending free, age-appropriate books to young children in her hometown before expanding across the United States and other countries.

The program has since grown into a global literacy effort, with more than 270 million books mailed to children as of 2026. Its reach has made Parton synonymous with childhood literacy, earning her the affectionate nickname “The Book Lady.”

Parton’s charitable work has also extended to communities affected by disasters. Following the 2016 wildfires in Sevier County, Tennessee, which destroyed thousands of structures and killed 14 people, Parton and the Dollywood Foundation established the My People Fund. The initiative provided $1,000 a month for six months to families whose homes were damaged or rendered uninhabitable. It ultimately raised more than $9 million for wildfire survivors, while a subsequent partnership with the Mountain Tough Recovery Team provided an additional $3 million for longer-term recovery.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Parton donated $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center for research into the coronavirus. Her contribution supported research that became part of the work that led to Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccine, making her one of the notable entertainment figures whose philanthropy helped advance vaccine research.

She also made major donations to pediatric infectious disease research. In early 2026, the East Tennessee Children’s Hospital announced it was naming its campus the Dolly Parton Children’s Hospital in honor of her ongoing support.

Her commitment to disaster relief continued in 2024 after Hurricane Helene devastated parts of the southeastern United States, including East Tennessee and western North Carolina. Parton pledged $1 million of her own money to the Mountain Ways Foundation, with her East Tennessee businesses, including Dollywood, matching the contribution and bringing the total from her side to $2 million.

Her philanthropy has earned major recognition, including the Library of Congress’ David M. Rubenstein Prize for her work through the Imagination Library. In 2022, she also received the Carnegie Medal of Philanthropy, which recognized her contributions to education, poverty alleviation and medical research, among other causes.

articles.title: Keeping flu protection within reach: Watsons makes vaccination more accessible to Filipinos
articles.summary: With frequent rain and the rainy season, many Filipinos are finding themselves moving between rainy streets, air-conditioned spaces, and crowded areas as they go about their daily routines. While flu…

blocks.text: With frequent rain and the rainy season, many Filipinos are finding themselves moving between rainy streets, air-conditioned spaces, and crowded areas as they go about their daily routines. While flu remains a year-round health concern, the rainy season serves as a timely reminder to pay closer attention to respiratory health and the preventive steps that can help protect ourselves and our loved ones.

Flu can begin with symptoms that may seem simple or familiar, such as fever, cough, colds, sore throat, headache, or body aches. Most people recover without serious complications, but some may be more vulnerable to severe illness, including older adults, young children, pregnant women, and people with certain underlying health conditions. Staying informed and taking preventive measures, including flu vaccination, can therefore be an important part of maintaining good health.

For many Filipinos, however, knowing what to do is only part of the challenge. Busy work schedules, school activities, family responsibilities, and everyday errands can make it easy to put preventive healthcare on hold, especially when getting vaccinated means making a separate trip to a healthcare facility.

Watsons is helping make vaccination more accessible by bringing these services closer to where Filipinos already live, work, and shop. Vaccination services are available at more than 300 Watsons stores nationwide, many of which are located in SM Malls. Of these, 22 vaccination hubs offer daily services, giving individuals and families greater flexibility and more opportunities to make preventive care part of their regular routines, at a time that works for them.

More than 85,000 patients have already received vaccinations through Watsons, reflecting the growing demand for accessible preventive healthcare. Among the vaccines offered, flu vaccines remain the most in demand, followed by HPV, pneumonia, shingles, and pertussis vaccines.

“We understand that with busy schedules, preventive care can sometimes be put off, so we continue to make vaccination services more accessible through our stores. With flu vaccines among the most in-demand vaccines, and as the rainy season continues, we hope to give more Filipinos the flexibility to get vaccinated as part of their everyday routines and take an important step toward protecting themselves and their loved ones,” said Danilo S. Chiong, Managing Director of Watsons.

Beyond vaccination, simple everyday practices such as washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes, and staying home when feeling unwell can also help reduce the spread of respiratory illnesses. Those experiencing severe, persistent, or worsening symptoms should seek appropriate medical advice.

Whether you’re heading to work, bringing the kids to school, or simply doing your weekly errands, staying protected against the flu can be one simple step toward keeping yourself and your loved ones healthy.
For the latest updates on vaccination schedules and participating stores, customers can also follow Watsons Philippines on social media or visit the Watsons website.

articles.title: PH urged to push Asean action vs harmful social media content
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Internet security watchdog Scam Watch Pilipinas urged the Philippine government to push the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to take joint action against harmful…

blocks.caption: A man uses a smartphone as various social media apps are displayed on screen in Pugoda on June 12, 2026. FILE PHOTO/Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Internet security watchdog Scam Watch Pilipinas urged the Philippine government to push the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) to take joint action against harmful content on social media.

“For too long, countries like the Philippines have been dealing with the world’s biggest technology companies individually,” Scam Watch Pilipinas lead convenor Jocel de Guzman said in a statement on Wednesday.

“When we ask platforms to act on harmful content, scam advertisements, fake accounts or other digital threats, cooperation often depends on the willingness of the platform because our jurisdiction and enforcement reach are limited,” he added.
He cited that the Philippines currently chairs the Asean.

On Tuesday, Sen. Erwin Tulfo slammed social media companies for allowing the spread of content from the fatal school shootings in Tacloban City last June 22 and in Zamboanga City last August 18 despite the sites’ existing community standards.
The Tacloban shooting was perpetrated by two teenagers and left three students dead, while the Zamboanga shooting was perpetrated by a lone teenager and left him and another schoolmate dead.
The latter incident had been livestreamed by the gunman on his Facebook account and on another livestreaming platform, the footage of which has since circulated online.

Meanwhile, in Thailand last August 7, after reportedly being exposed to violent content and learning to use a gun on social media, another teenage gunman had opened fire inside a school and killed himself and six other people.
“Big Tech operates across borders… harmful content spreads across borders. Regulation cannot remain trapped within national borders,” de Guzman stressed.
“If Big Tech wants access to nearly 700 million Asean consumers, accountability to those same consumers cannot be optional,” he added.
The Scam Watch Pilipinas lead convenor also responded to calls by government officials to implement a ban on social media for minor users in the wake of the shootings.
“Blocking should not be our default answer,” he said.
“The better solution is to strengthen the ability of governments to regulate these companies, compel cooperation and hold them accountable when they repeatedly fail to act,” he added.

At the Asean Chiefs of Police (Aseanapol) conference last July, the Philippine National Police (PNP) said it was considering a recommendation for the country to adopt a measure similar to Australia’s social media ban for users aged 16 and younger.
Following the Zamboanga shooting, the Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center said it was also considering recommending a ban on Facebook in the country.

articles.title: Duterte Impeachment Trial: Who is Prosecution Counsel Amando Virgil Ligutan?
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Amando Virgil Ligutan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte. Since the trial began,…

blocks.caption: Atty. Amando Virgil Ligutan at the Senate impeachment court.  | INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Lawyer Amando Virgil Ligutan is among the private lawyers assisting the House prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Since the trial began, Ligutan has conducted the prosecution’s direct examination of National Bureau of Investigation Regional Director Jeremy Lotoc and Gina Acosta, a former special disbursing officer of the Office of the Vice President who testified as a hostile witness.
The Cebuano lawyer is not afraid to use his native language during trial, even at times translating for Acosta when the latter said she found some Tagalog words quite deep.
Ligutan is the managing partner of SALiGAL Law (Sapayan Lim Alvarez & Ligutan Law Offices) in Cebu.

He is also actively teaching Labor Law, Remedial Law, and Public International Law as a lecturer and law instructor in University of the Philippines, University of San Jose-Recoletos School of Law, and University of Cebu School of Law.
Ligutan was valedictorian when he graduated High School from Sacred Heart Seminary in Palo Leyte in 1999.
Four years later, he completed his undergraduate degree in AB Philosophy from University of San Carlos in Cebu, and was awarded Summa Cum Laude.
He then pursued Law in University of the Philippines Diliman and graduated in 2009.
Among his expertise are civil and criminal litigation, political and administrative law, and public interest cases.
He also has expertise in labor relations law, risk and crisis management, and local government and election law.

This Wednesday, Aug. 26, Ligutan is set to explain his Facebook post, which read, “A principle all lawyers and law students know by heart: Misleading questions are not allowed even on cross-examination.”

The post became a point of concern when defense lead counsel Sheila Sison raised to the impeachment court that the post was seemingly referring to a statement made by defense counsel Kristine Ferrer during her cross-examination of state auditor Xylene del Campo.

NEW YORK — Mirra Andreeva revealed a secret Tuesday after she and Andrey Rublev ended the reign of the two-time US Open mixed doubles champions.
She used to have a crush on her partner.
“I’ve never said anything, I’ve never told him anything as well, but I used to have a little crush on him as well,” Andreeva said during an interview on the court.
That’s just adorable 🤗 pic.twitter.com/R3bunVJUzj — US Open Tennis (@usopen) August 25, 2026

The French Open champion added that it was “like a dream come true to play with my favorite” before being unable to finish that sentence when Rublev interrupted to give her a hug as the crowd cheered.

The crush is over — the 19-year-old Andreeva said it was when she was 15 or 16 — but their tournament goes on. The Russians will play Wednesday night in the semifinals against Karolina Muchova and Jakub Mensik.
They began the event by outlasting Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori 1-4, 4-1 (11-9), then emerged from another match tiebreaker to edge Diana Shnaider and Casper Ruud for their semifinal spot.
Rublev, 28, is perhaps most recognizable for his red hair and his occasional outbursts on the court. Andreeva definitely noticed his appearance, but thought he was kind despite the tirades.
“I mean, first of all, his hair, OK?” she responded when asked why she was drawn to him.

articles.title: From Strategy to Execution: Powering Central Luzon’s AI future through regional digital transformation
articles.summary: The Department of Science and Technology Regional Office No. III (DOST-III / DOST-CL) and WPH Digital, a Singapore-based AI and digital innovation company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding…

blocks.text: The Department of Science and Technology Regional Office No. III (DOST-III / DOST-CL) and WPH Digital, a Singapore-based AI and digital innovation company, have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to accelerate regional digital transformation and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption across Central Luzon.

The collaboration brings the Philippines’ National Artificial Intelligence Strategy (NAIS-PH) closer to regional implementation by combining DOST-III’s public-sector mandate with WPH Digital’s expertise in AI, digital transformation, and practical technology implementation.

The agreement was formally signed by Dr. Julius Ceasar V. Sicat, Regional Director of DOST Central Luzon, and Mr. Vincent Leoh, Managing Director of WPH Digital, on 19 August 2026. Held at the opening of the joint program, the ceremony was witnessed by over 50 key delegates and industry leaders representing diverse business, technology, and public sectors from across Central Luzon.

“We believe AI adoption is not a technology challenge — it is a capability challenge,” said Mr. Vincent Leoh, Managing Director of WPH Digital. “Through WPH Academy, we help people build AI capabilities, and through WPH Digital, we help organisations apply those capabilities using practical AI solutions. When capability building and practical implementation come together, organisations start seeing real value from AI.”
Democratizing Generative AI Across Central Luzon

By bringing enterprise-grade digital expertise directly to Region III, the collaboration demonstrates how government and private-sector organisations can work together to democratize access to advanced Generative AI and cloud computing technologies beyond Metro Manila. The initiative positions Central Luzon as a key regional innovation hub, driving competitiveness across local micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs), industries, and public sector operations.
Human Capital and Workforce Readiness First

At the heart of the partnership is a strong emphasis on talent reskilling, practical capability-building, and workforce development. Rather than viewing technology solely as a displacement risk, the collaboration equips local professionals and civil servants to use Generative AI as a productivity multiplier—fostering a resilient, highly competitive regional talent pool equipped for modern, future-ready workflows.

As an immediate step toward putting the partnership into action, DOST-III and WPH Digital conducted the Generative AI for Modern Business Operations workshop. The practical capacity-building session provided business leaders, IT professionals, and regional stakeholders with hands-on exposure to practical AI solutions, cloud-native platforms, and execution strategies designed to deliver practical business value.

Beyond training and capability-building, the collaboration is intended to help organisations translate these capabilities into actual implementation, enabling them to identify practical AI opportunities and develop solutions that can be applied within their operating environments.
International Cross-Border Tech Collaboration

The MOU highlights cross-border technology transfer between Singapore’s private sector and the Philippine government. By bringing Singaporean tech consulting expertise to Central Luzon, WPH Digital showcases how international private-sector solutions can actively contribute to regional development goals in organisations and communities across Southeast Asia.

“AI is already here, and it is becoming part of how businesses plan, create, communicate, and improve their operations,” said Dr. Julius Caesar V. Sicat, Regional Director of DOST Central Luzon. “This training is not just about learning AI — it is about empowering our MSMEs to confidently embrace change and turn technology into opportunities.”
Trusted AI with Certified Governance

The partnership also underscores the importance of responsible and governed AI adoption as organisations move from experimentation to implementation. WPH Digital brings AI governance expertise backed by the internationally recognised ISO/IEC 42001 standard, which provides a structured framework for responsible, secure, ethical, and governed AI adoption.
WPH Digital is one of the first AI and Digital Service Providers in Singapore to achieve ISO/IEC 42001 certification for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems, and is the first in the world

to achieve ISO/IEC 42001 certification for AI systems in the oil and gas industry. This experience supports the company’s approach to helping organisations move beyond AI concepts and strategy toward practical, production-ready solutions.

By combining AI expertise, enterprise technology experience, cloud capabilities, and ISO/IEC 42001-based AI governance, WPH Digital brings an implementation-focused approach to AI adoption. Under the DOST-III partnership, this approach complements workforce training and technical capability-building, helping organisations explore how AI can be applied responsibly and effectively within their operating environments.
A Replicable Blueprint for Regional Action

The alliance establishes a repeatable model for regional government-industry partnerships throughout the Philippines. Moving beyond high-level strategy, DOST-III and WPH Digital provide a structured model for continuous technical implementation, capacity building, and enterprise enablement across provincial economies.

The longer-term ambition is for this model to extend from national government agencies to provincial and local government units (LGUs), and eventually across other regions of the Philippines. By connecting national AI priorities with regional capability-building and practical implementation, the collaboration has the potential to provide a scalable model for AI capabilities.

blocks.text: On the night of Aug. 27-28, a partial lunar eclipse will be visible across the country.
The eclipse comes roughly two weeks after the total solar eclipse that was seen across Iceland, Spain and a small portion of Portugal.
While this will be a partial eclipse, it will be a deep one, with 93 per cent coverage at its maximum.

Lunar eclipses occur when the moon moves through Earth’s shadow, called its umbra. Before it enters the umbra, however, it passes through Earth’s outer, dimmer shadow, called the penumbra. However, because it is much dimmer, it’s difficult to see with the naked eye when this occurs.

blocks.text: Most of Canada will see the entire duration of the eclipse, while Western Canada will see the partial eclipse already taking place as the moon rises.

blocks.text: The great news is that, unlike with a solar eclipse, you don’t need any protective eyewear to watch the event.

blocks.text: When to see it
The eclipse will begin as the moon enters Earth’s penumbra at roughly 10 p.m. ET, but that’s not when you want to go out to start observing.

Instead, the visible part of the eclipse begins at 10:33 p.m. ET on Aug. 27 and ends at 1:52 a.m. on Aug. 28. The deepest part of the eclipse will occur at 12:13 a.m. with almost all of the moon appearing darkened.
This is just one of many astronomical events taking place this month.

"It's kind of a fun one because … August had so many great things going on for it and still does," said Elaina Hyde, director of the Allan I. Carswell Observatory York University’s department of physics and astronomy in Toronto.

"We had, of course, the very, very partial solar eclipse back on August 12th. We had the Perseids, which were either fabulous or slightly less fabulous, depending on how cloudy your skies were. And, of course, the Jupiter-Mercury conjunction."
Will it be a "blood moon"?
"It's a partial eclipse, so it's not going to turn 100 per cent red, but depending on where you are in Canada, it will still be pretty red," Hyde said.
The great thing about lunar eclipses is that there's no need for any equipment — just your eyes.
"This is a naked eye object, but if you have binoculars or a small telescope or just a [cellphone] camera with a really good night mode, you should be able to get pretty good pictures," Hyde said.
